record.description: Dimensionless ratio comparing a particle species’ kinetic temperature with the positive reference temperature on the same magnetic flux surface.
record.documentation:
The quantity expresses the kinetic temperature of a selected particle species relative to a single reference thermal scale on the same magnetic flux surface. It is the normalized counterpart of [particle temperature](name:particle_temperature), while retaining the species dependence of the numerator.

It is defined by

$$
T_p^{\mathrm{norm}} = \frac{T_p}{T_{\mathrm{ref}}}
$$

where $T_p$ is the kinetic temperature of the selected particle species and $T_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the positive reference temperature for the flux surface.

The ratio is dimensionless and is not an absolute temperature; its value depends on the specified reference temperature.
record.name: ratio_of_particle_temperature_to_particle_reference_temperature

record.description: Lower-bound photon energy sets the low-energy cutoff for X-ray photon counting, admitting only photons above the threshold of the specified detector pixel or channel. For an energy-resolved emission band, the bound instead specifies the low-energy boundary of the included emission and is assumed common to all channels used in the profile reconstruction. Values are expressed in eV, stored as a two-dimensional per-pixel array for the X-ray camera and as a scalar for each detector-channel energy band or emissivity-profile energy band.
record.documentation:
Lower-bound photon energy is the low-energy edge of an X-ray detection or emission band. For photon counting, it is the threshold that an incident photon must exceed to be eligible for registration.

The lower-threshold requirement for counting is:

$$
E_{\gamma} > E_{\gamma,\min}
$$

where $E_{\gamma}$ is the incident photon energy and $E_{\gamma,\min}$ is the lower photon-energy threshold assigned to the specified detector pixel or channel.

The counting threshold applies individually to that pixel or channel, rather than representing an average over the detector. For an energy-resolved emission band, the bound instead specifies the low-energy boundary of the included emission.

Together with [upper photon energy](name:upper_photon_energy), this bound specifies the spectral window. It is a band boundary, not a [central or representative pixel photon energy](name:energy_of_detector_pixel). Exceeding the lower threshold is necessary for counting but does not imply unit detection probability.
record.name: lower_bound_photon_energy

record.description: Effective turn count of a passive loop element is the signed number of equivalent windings assigned to a passive axisymmetric conducting loop element for electromagnetic coupling in calculating magnetic fields of the coil/loop. It weights the passive-loop current contribution and may be fractional for equivalent or homogenized loop elements. Positive means current is counter-clockwise when seen from above. It is a dimensionless scalar with unit 1.
record.documentation:
Effective turn count of a passive loop element is the signed number of equivalent windings assigned to a passive conducting loop element for electromagnetic coupling. It may be fractional when the represented conductor is an equivalent or homogenized passive-loop element rather than a literal winding. Positive means current is counter-clockwise when seen from above.

The signed current-turn source strength represented by the passive loop element is defined by:

$$
\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{loop}} = N_{\mathrm{eff}} I_{\mathrm{loop}}
$$

where $\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{loop}}$ is the signed current-turn source strength of the passive loop element, $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is the effective turn count of the passive loop element, and $I_{\mathrm{loop}}$ is the [current of the passive loop](name:current_of_passive_loop).

This quantity applies to the represented passive-loop element as one electromagnetic circuit contribution. Each loop is comprised of a number of cross-section elements described individually. It has no implicit aggregation over multiple passive loops; if several represented windings or conductor pieces are collapsed into one loop element, their net orientation and coupling are represented by the single algebraic value of $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$.

It is distinct from the [current of the passive loop](name:current_of_passive_loop), which is multiplied by $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$, and from the [area of the passive loop](name:area_of_passive_loop), which describes conductor cross section. It is not a turn count for magnetic probes, coil conductor elements, toroidal-field coils, or magnetic field-line winding.
record.name: effective_turn_count_of_passive_loop_element

The resulting name, "motional_stark_polarization_angle_at_constraint_position", already appears among the neighbours with the definition "Polarization angle of Stark-split Balmer-alpha light from neutral-beam atoms at a constraint position specifies its linear-polarization orientation for the selected viewing geometry." record.description: Polarization angle of motional Stark effect emission at a constraint position: the angular orientation of the linear-polarization axis of the beam emission for the specified neutral-beam and viewing geometry, whether realized as an observed angle or as the angle consistent with a reconstructed equilibrium state.
record.documentation:
Polarization angle of motional Stark effect emission at a constraint position is the angular orientation of the linear-polarization axis of the light emitted by injected neutral-beam atoms, for the specified neutral-beam and viewing geometry.

The polarization angle is defined by

$$
\alpha = \operatorname{atan2}\!\left(\hat{\mathbf p}\cdot\hat{\mathbf e}_2,\;\hat{\mathbf p}\cdot\hat{\mathbf e}_1\right) \pmod{\pi}
$$

where $\alpha$ is the polarization angle, $\hat{\mathbf p}$ is a unit vector along the linear-polarization axis of the emission, and $\hat{\mathbf e}_1$ and $\hat{\mathbf e}_2$ are orthonormal unit vectors spanning the viewing plane perpendicular to the line of sight: $\hat{\mathbf e}_1$ sets the angular zero and $\hat{\mathbf e}_2$ sets the positive angular direction. Reduction modulo a half-turn reflects that linear polarization defines an axis rather than an oriented vector, so orientations differing by a half-turn are equivalent.

The quantity is specific to the constraint position and to the stated beam and viewing geometry; it is not an average over positions, beams, or sightlines. It may denote the observed emission polarization orientation or the orientation that a reconstructed equilibrium state implies for the same geometry; both realizations denote the same physical angle.

It is not a residual between observed and equilibrium-consistent values, not a statistical weight, and not the magnetic-field pitch angle: the correspondence between this angle and the local magnetic-field pitch depends on the beam velocity, the viewing geometry, and the selected Stark polarization component. It is a geometry-specific form of the polarization angle, and it differs from the [Faraday angle](name:faraday_angle), which is a propagation-induced rotation of polarization rather than an emission polarization orientation.

Sign convention: Positive when the polarization axis rotates from the zero-angle reference direction $\hat{\mathbf e}_1$ toward the positive reference direction $\hat{\mathbf e}_2$ within the viewing plane.
record.name: polarization_angle_at_constraint_position

reason: The source specifies “Normalised collisionality between two species”, and the recorded source qualification is normalization to “a characteristic transit frequency”, not the incumbent's “streaming, transit, or bounce frequency”. The bound source also states “ndim=2”, which must appear in the definition.

record.description: Dimensionless ratio of a specified interspecies collision frequency to the characteristic transit frequency used for the plasma population. It is represented as a two-dimensional array indexed by the two particle species and has unit 1.
record.documentation:
This collisionality measures the strength of interspecies collisional relaxation relative to collisionless motion along magnetic-field trajectories.

$$
\nu_{ab}^{*} = \frac{\nu_{ab}}{\omega_{\mathrm{char}}}
$$

where $\nu_{ab}$ is the collision frequency between species $a$ and $b$, and $\omega_{\mathrm{char}}$ is the relevant characteristic transit frequency; both quantities have reciprocal-time units.

The denominator must be interpreted as the characteristic transit frequency for the selected plasma population, so this quantity is distinct from the collision frequency itself. It generalizes the population-specific electron collisionality and complements collisionality at the pedestal top when the characteristic frequency is evaluated there.
record.name: normalized_interspecies_collisionality

record.description: Thermodynamic temperature associated with a selected thermocouple sensor attached to a tokamak structural component.
record.documentation:
This quantity is the absolute thermodynamic temperature associated with one selected sensor member, represented by the thermal state at its thermocouple junction. It characterizes the local thermal condition of the attached structural component at the sensor location.

For a system in thermodynamic equilibrium, temperature is defined by

$$
T = \left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial S}\right)_{V,N}
$$

where $T$ is thermodynamic temperature, $U$ is internal energy, $S$ is entropy, $V$ is volume, and $N$ is the amount of material or particle number held fixed in the derivative.

The quantity applies to the selected sensor member individually and is not a sum, average, or other aggregation over the sensor set. It denotes the sensor or junction thermal state associated with a structural component, not the temperature of a flowing coolant or of an entire plant connection.

It is distinct from [coolant temperature at inlet](name:coolant_temperature_at_inlet), which describes fluid entering a cooling system. Object-specific quantities such as [temperature of a coil conductor](name:temperature_of_coil_conductor) and [temperature of a neutron detector](name:temperature_of_neutron_detector) apply the same thermodynamic concept to explicitly named hardware rather than to the generic sensor locus.
record.name: temperature_of_sensor

The definition omits numerical details specified by “Normalised toroidal beta, defined as 100 * beta_tor * a[m] * B0 [T] / ip [MA]”, the pressure method specified by “using the pressure determined by an equilibrium reconstruction code”, and the averaging and pressure component identified by “volume-averaged total perpendicular plasma pressure”. The enclosing structures specify “0D parameters of the equilibrium” and “Set of equilibria at various time slices”; the profile-derived and summary sources specify “ndim=1”. These details must be explicit in the definition.

record.description:
Normalized toroidal beta is the whole-plasma toroidal pressure beta rescaled by minor radius and signed reference toroidal field relative to plasma current. It is dimensionless (unit 1), with defining normalization beta_N = 100 * beta_tor * a[m] * B0[T] / Ip[MA], where a is the positive plasma minor radius, B0 is the nonzero signed reference vacuum toroidal magnetic field and Ip is the nonzero signed net toroidal plasma current; their numerical values are taken in metres, teslas and megaamperes, respectively. The underlying beta_tor = 2*mu_0*

/B0^2 uses vacuum permeability mu_0 and the whole-plasma volume average

of total perpendicular plasma pressure, including the represented thermal and nonthermal contributions. For the equilibrium-reconstruction variant, the pressure is determined by an equilibrium reconstruction code without changing the normalization. The signed ratio B0/Ip is preserved. The quantity is a global scalar evaluated at each equilibrium time slice; the bound profile-derived and summary representations are one-dimensional arrays.
record.documentation:
Normalized toroidal beta is the conventional current-and-geometry rescaling of the whole-plasma toroidal pressure beta. Its defining normalization is $\beta_{\mathrm{N}}=100\,\beta_{\mathrm{tor}}\,a[\mathrm{m}]\,B_0[\mathrm{T}]/I_p[\mathrm{MA}]$. Here $\beta_{\mathrm{N}}$ is normalized toroidal beta, $\beta_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the dimensionless [toroidal beta](name:toroidal_beta), $a$ is plasma minor radius, $B_0$ is the signed reference vacuum toroidal magnetic field and $I_p$ is the signed net toroidal plasma current. The bracketed units specify the numerical values used in this conventional normalization.

The underlying toroidal pressure ratio, before that rescaling, obeys $$\beta = \frac{2\mu_0 \langle p\rangle}{B^2}$$ with $\beta=\beta_{\mathrm{tor}}$, $B=B_0$, $\mu_0$ vacuum permeability and $\langle p\rangle$ the whole-plasma volume average of the total perpendicular pressure $p$ used to form the toroidal beta. This pressure-ratio equation defines the operand $\beta_{\mathrm{tor}}$; it is not the defining equation of $\beta_{\mathrm{N}}$.

The pressure input includes the thermal and nonthermal contributions represented by the total-pressure input. A pressure estimate obtained from equilibrium reconstruction changes that pressure input rather than the normalization. Restricting the pressure input to thermal pressure defines the separately named [normalized toroidal thermal beta](name:normalized_toroidal_thermal_beta).

The normalization requires positive minor radius and nonzero reference field and plasma current. It preserves the signed ratio $B_0/I_p$ without silently replacing either by its magnitude. For nonnegative underlying toroidal beta, the sign of the normalized value follows that ratio. The normalized quantity differs from unnormalized toroidal beta by the explicit factor of 100 and the stated size, field and current factors.
record.name: normalized_toroidal_beta

reason: The limiter registry states: “At the limiter, a measurement refers to the scrape-off-layer plasma immediately adjacent to its surface; the precise plasma evaluation point is not specified.” This contradicts the incumbent's specified magnetic-presheath or sheath-entrance evaluation point. The bound source specifies “unit=m^-3”.

record.description: Local particle number density of hydrogen ions in the boundary plasma immediately adjacent to a plasma-facing limiter surface; the precise plasma evaluation point is not specified. The unit is m^-3.
record.documentation:
Hydrogen density at a limiter is the local number density of hydrogen ions in the boundary plasma immediately adjacent to a plasma-facing limiter surface. The precise plasma evaluation point is not specified; neutral hydrogen is excluded. For hydrogen, the charge-state sum reduces to the density of positively charged hydrogen ions, H+.

The local hydrogen-ion density is defined from the velocity distribution function:

$$
n_{\mathrm{H}^+} = \int f_{\mathrm{H}^+}(\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{H}^+}$ is the hydrogen-ion number density, $f_{\mathrm{H}^+}$ is the hydrogen-ion velocity distribution function, and $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity at the evaluation point.

This quantity is the hydrogen-specific component of [density_at_limiter](name:density_at_limiter). It counts hydrogen ions separately from [deuterium_density_at_limiter](name:deuterium_density_at_limiter), and does not include neutral hydrogen or other ion species.
record.name: hydrogen_density_at_limiter

reason: The adjudicator states that “back_surface_neutron_flux” denotes “neutron number flux,” whereas the definition specifies “neutron kinetic-energy transfer” and “not a neutron count flux.” Adding energy to the name identifies the explicitly defined quantity while retaining its correct energy-flux unit: “The stored unit ‘W.m^-2’ fits energy flux.”

record.description: Back-surface neutron energy flux is the local rate of neutron kinetic-energy transfer outward through an object's designated rear surface, per unit actual surface area and time. It is a scalar energy flux, not a neutron count flux, integrated power, or spatial maximum. Its unit is W.m^-2.
record.documentation:
Back-surface neutron energy flux is the local rate at which neutron kinetic energy crosses outward through an object's designated rear surface, per unit actual surface area and time. It is a scalar measure of energy transfer, not a neutron count rate.

The local energy flux is defined by

$$
\Gamma_{n,\mathrm{back}}^{E}(\mathbf r,t) = \frac{\partial^2 E_{n,\mathrm{out}}}{\partial A\,\partial t}(\mathbf r,t)
$$

where $\Gamma_{n,\mathrm{back}}^{E}$ is the back-surface neutron energy flux, $n$ identifies the neutron contributions, $\mathbf r$ is position on the back surface, $t$ is time, $E_{n,\mathrm{out}}$ is the cumulative kinetic energy carried by neutrons crossing outward through the surface, and $A$ is actual surface area.

The quantity applies locally over the object's designated back surface and aggregates the kinetic-energy contributions of outward-crossing neutrons across their energies. It excludes neutron number flux, neutron production within a volume, energy deposited inside material, power integrated over a surface, and a spatial maximum or average over the surface.

Integrating the local flux over a portion of the back surface gives the neutron power crossing outward through that portion. The [maximum of back-surface neutron flux](name:maximum_of_back_surface_neutron_flux) is the greatest local value over the applicable back surface; that maximum is not part of this local quantity.
record.name: back_surface_neutron_energy_flux

record.description: Characteristic timescale of electric-current decrease during a disruption, defined by a specified linear-threshold or exponential decay convention.
record.documentation:
This quantity characterizes electric-current decay during a disruption. It encompasses the total plasma current and the current carried by a specified particle population, without imposing a particular current component or decay convention.

For a linear threshold convention, the extrapolated full-decay time is defined by:

$$
\tau_{\mathrm{lin}}=\frac{t(f_{\mathrm{low}})-t(f_{\mathrm{high}})}{f_{\mathrm{high}}-f_{\mathrm{low}}}
$$

where $\tau_{\mathrm{lin}}$ is the linear decay time, $f_{\mathrm{high}}$ and $f_{\mathrm{low}}$ are the upper and lower fractions of a specified reference current magnitude, and $t(f)$ is the time at which the decaying current magnitude reaches fraction $f$ of that reference.

An exponential convention instead defines an e-folding time through $I(t)=I_0\exp[-(t-t_0)/\tau_{\mathrm{exp}}]$, where $I(t)$ is the selected current magnitude at time $t$, $I_0$ is its value at reference time $t_0$, and $\tau_{\mathrm{exp}}$ is the exponential decay time. A linear threshold time is not generally equal to an exponential e-folding time.

The [plasma-current decay time](name:plasma_decay_time_due_to_disruption) uses the linear construction with upper and lower fractions of 0.8 and 0.2. The [runaway-electron current decay time](name:runaway_electron_decay_time_due_to_disruption) applies to the total toroidal runaway-electron current and permits custom linear, fixed 20–80% linear, or exponential conventions. These specializations characterize different current populations and need not have equal decay times; neither denotes a local current-density decay time or an electron-temperature decay time.
record.name: decay_time_due_to_disruption

record.description: Major-radius coordinate of a reference point in a poloidal-field coil's cross-sectional geometry, measured by perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis.
record.documentation:
Major-radius coordinate of poloidal field coil

This coil-specific instance of the [radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate) is defined by

$$
R = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}
$$

where $x$ and $y$ are the transverse coordinates of the same point in a right-handed Cartesian $(x, y, z)$ frame whose $z$ axis coincides with the toroidal symmetry axis and whose vertical coordinate is $z=Z$.

The coordinate is nonnegative and applies to the specified geometric reference point, which need not coincide with the coil center. It is a point location, not an average over the coil or a cross-sectional radius. Unlike the [radial outline of the poloidal-field coil](name:radial_outline_of_poloidal_field_coil), it does not describe the complete cross-sectional boundary.
record.name: radial_coordinate_of_poloidal_field_coil

reason: The definition omits numerical conventions specified elsewhere in the case file: “The contribution is defined by Faraday's law” with “V_{\mathrm{ext}}(t) = -\frac{d\Phi_{\mathrm{ext}}(t)}{dt}”; “the externally generated poloidal magnetic flux linked by the considered toroidal plasma circuit”; “It excludes resistive voltage drops and other non-inductive contributions”; and “Positive when the induced electromotive force has a positive line integral in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.” The recorded reason also specifies a “global 0-D equilibrium quantity”.

record.description: Electromotive-force contribution to the plasma loop voltage caused by changing externally generated poloidal magnetic flux, including flux linked through active coils and passive conducting structures. This global, zero-dimensional scalar is V_ext(t) = -dΦ_ext(t)/dt, where Φ_ext(t) is the externally generated poloidal magnetic flux linked by the considered toroidal plasma circuit and t is time; its unit is V. It excludes resistive voltage drops and other non-inductive contributions. Positive when the induced electromotive force has a positive line integral in the direction of increasing toroidal angle φ in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
record.documentation:
This quantity is the inductive electromotive-force contribution to the plasma loop voltage produced by time-varying poloidal magnetic flux generated by active coil circuits and magnetically coupled passive conducting structures. It excludes resistive voltage drops and other non-inductive contributions.

The contribution is defined by Faraday's law:

$$
V_{\mathrm{ext}}(t) = -\frac{d\Phi_{\mathrm{ext}}(t)}{dt}
$$

where $\Phi_{\mathrm{ext}}$ is the externally generated poloidal magnetic flux linked by the considered toroidal plasma circuit and $t$ is time. It contributes to the total [loop voltage at the plasma boundary](name:loop_voltage_at_plasma_boundary); currents in passive conductors are represented by the linked-flux response of structures such as those described by [current of passive structure](name:current_of_passive_structure).

Sign convention: Positive when the induced electromotive force has a positive line integral in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.
record.name: external_loop_voltage

reason: The source says "Minimum flow rate of the valve", identifying the valve locus omitted from the incumbent name. The supplied neighbour "gas_flow_of_valve" establishes that locus construction, and the qualifier vocabulary supplies "lower_bound" rather than "minimum". The definition now explicitly includes the documented calculation "Q_g = p_g \frac{dV_g}{dt}" and the source unit "Pa.m^3.s^-1".

record.description: Minimum gas flow is the smallest pressure-volume gas throughput that a gas injection valve can reliably deliver, defining the lower bound of its controllable range. Pressure-volume throughput is p_g dV_g/dt, where p_g is gas pressure at the flow boundary and dV_g/dt is the volumetric flow rate across that boundary; the unit is Pa.m^3.s^-1.
record.documentation:
Minimum gas flow is the lower reliable operating limit of the pressure-volume throughput delivered by a gas injection valve. It identifies the smallest controllable value of the aggregate gas stream throughput, rather than a molecular-species flow or particle-number rate.

The pressure-volume throughput represented by this quantity is defined as

$$
Q_g = p_g \frac{dV_g}{dt}
$$

where $Q_g$ is gas pressure-volume throughput, $p_g$ is gas pressure at the flow boundary, $V_g$ is the volume of gas crossing that boundary, and $t$ is time.

This quantity applies to the aggregate gas stream delivered through an injection system across a defined flow boundary. The stream is not restricted to a particular molecular species or charge state, and this quantity is distinct from mass flow and particle-number rate. Its defining distinction is the lower reliable operating bound, rather than an unrestricted instantaneous throughput.

The gas flow quantity defines the same pressure-volume throughput without imposing a lower-limit condition; minimum gas flow is its lower reliable operating bound. Conversely, [maximum gas flow](name:maximum_gas_flow) is the upper reliable operating bound, so the two quantities delimit the controllable range rather than represent different throughput definitions.
record.name: lower_bound_gas_flow_of_valve

reason: The adjudicator identifies “Radial drift of the pellet deposition location relative to the ablation location,” while the bound source specifies “between the ablation and the final deposition locations, in terms of the normalised toroidal flux coordinate”; this is not a toroidal displacement. The enclosing structures specify “1-D profiles of plasma and pellet along the pellet path” and “The time of this structure corresponds to the full ablation of the pellet inside the plasma.” These require the deposition-relative-to-ablation name and the explicit profile and time-slice qualifications in the definition; the coordinate normalisation remains in the definition.

record.description: Shift of pellet-material deposition relative to its ablation location caused by E×B drift, expressed as a difference in normalized toroidal flux coordinate. The difference is final deposition minus ablation, evaluated for material ablated at each corresponding location in a one-dimensional profile along the pellet path, not integrated along the path. The time slice corresponds to full ablation of the pellet inside the plasma. The unit is 1.
record.documentation:
The pellet deposition displacement describes the shift of ablated pellet material from its ablation location to its final deposition location attributable to E-cross-B drift. It is expressed as a difference in normalized toroidal flux coordinate.

The displacement is defined by deposition minus ablation:

$$
\Delta\rho_{\mathrm{tor},\mathrm{N}} = \rho_{\mathrm{tor},\mathrm{N},\mathrm{dep}} - \rho_{\mathrm{tor},\mathrm{N},\mathrm{abl}}
$$

where $\Delta\rho_{\mathrm{tor},\mathrm{N}}$ is the pellet deposition displacement, and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor},\mathrm{N},\mathrm{dep}}$ and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor},\mathrm{N},\mathrm{abl}}$ are the normalized toroidal flux coordinates at the final deposition and ablation locations, respectively.

Each value concerns material ablated at the corresponding location along the pellet path, not a path-integrated displacement. Only the shift attributed to E-cross-B drift is included. This coordinate difference is neither an absolute deposition coordinate nor a geometric distance or drift velocity; it describes redistribution of ablated material rather than the injection motion characterized by the [initial pellet velocity](name:initial_velocity_of_pellet).
record.name: radial_displacement_of_pellet_deposition_relative_to_ablation_due_to_e_cross_b_drift

reason: The source specifies “Thickness of this layer evaluated at the midplane”; the incumbent name, definition and documentation omit the midplane locus.

record.description: Non-negative geometric separation between the inner and outer material interfaces of a breeder blanket layer along the specified thickness direction, evaluated at the midplane, in m.
record.documentation:
Non-negative geometric separation between the inner and outer material interfaces of a breeder blanket layer is the local through-thickness of that layer along the specified thickness direction, evaluated at the midplane. The quantity applies to a single material or functional layer within the blanket, not to the total breeder blanket module build.

The layer thickness is defined by the separation of the two bounding interfaces along the thickness coordinate:

$$
d_\ell = \left|s_{\ell,\mathrm{out}} - s_{\ell,\mathrm{in}}\right|
$$

where $d_\ell$ is the layer thickness in m, and $s_{\ell,\mathrm{in}}$ and $s_{\ell,\mathrm{out}}$ are the signed coordinates in m of the inner and outer layer interfaces along the specified thickness direction.

It is not the toroidal width, poloidal height, surface extent, or volume-equivalent thickness of the layer. It is distinct from module-level quantities such as thickness_of_breeder_blanket_module, [lower_thickness_of_breeder_blanket_module](name:lower_thickness_of_breeder_blanket_module), and [upper_thickness_of_breeder_blanket_module](name:upper_thickness_of_breeder_blanket_module). For a radially stacked layer, the thickness direction is the cylindrical $\hat{R}$ direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.
record.name: thickness_of_breeder_blanket_layer_at_midplane

reason: The adjudicator states: "The name 'radius_of_poloidal_field_coil' identifies a coil radius, but the definition specifies the 'curvature radius of one arc-of-circle segment used to approximate the cross-sectional contour'—the local radius of a contour segment, not the radius of the coil." The name therefore needs the curvature distinction; the stated unit "m" is also made explicit in the definition.

record.description: Non-negative curvature radius, in m, of one arc-of-circle segment used to approximate the cross-sectional contour of a poloidal field coil. The contour lies in a poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, where R is major radius and Z is vertical height.
record.documentation:
Radius of a poloidal-field-coil arc is the non-negative circle radius of a single circular segment of the coil cross-sectional contour, taken in a poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. The conductor or winding-pack boundary is approximated by connected circular arcs, and this quantity sets the local radius of curvature of one such arc.

For a circular contour segment, the curvature radius $\rho$ (in m) is the inverse magnitude of the planar curvature $\kappa$ (in m$^{-1}$) of the boundary curve in the $(R, Z)$ cross-section:

$$
\rho = \frac{1}{|\kappa|}
$$

where a finite physical arc has $\rho > 0$, and as $\rho$ grows the segment approaches a straight line ($\kappa \to 0$). Each arc is anchored by a start point in the poloidal plane: its major-radius coordinate is given by major_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil and its vertical coordinate by [height_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:height_of_poloidal_field_coil); both together with $\rho$ are needed to locate and shape one arc, with the end of each arc coinciding with the start of the next.

The value is determined from the designed circular-arc contour, from CAD geometry, or by fitting circular arcs to surveyed boundary points. Small radii represent tightly rounded corners and compact winding-pack features, while larger radii represent gently curved coil sides; the magnitude scales with coil aperture, winding-pack dimensions, and mechanical-clearance requirements. An analogous arc-of-circle convention applies to iron core segment boundaries via radius_of_iron_core_segment.
record.name: curvature_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil

record.description: Orientation indicator equal to the sign of the toroidal magnetic-field component on a flux surface in local gyrokinetic geometry. It is the dimensionless scalar s_phi = B_phi/|B_phi|, where B_phi = B · phi_hat is the equilibrium magnetic-field component along increasing toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, with R the major radius and Z the vertical height. It equals +1 for a component directed toward increasing toroidal angle and -1 for the opposite direction, and is undefined when B_phi vanishes. Unit: 1.
record.documentation:
The toroidal magnetic-field sign specifies whether the equilibrium toroidal field component on a flux surface is directed along or opposite increasing toroidal angle in local gyrokinetic geometry.

For a nonzero toroidal magnetic-field component, the orientation indicator is defined by

$$
s_\phi = \operatorname{sgn}(B_\phi) = \frac{B_\phi}{|B_\phi|}
$$

where $s_\phi$ is the orientation indicator, $B_\phi$ is the toroidal magnetic-field component, and $\operatorname{sgn}$ is the sign function. The component is $B_\phi = \mathbf{B}\cdot\hat{\phi}$, where $\mathbf{B}$ is the equilibrium magnetic field and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector toward increasing toroidal angle. The right-handed cylindrical frame is $(R,\phi,Z)$, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

As the toroidal member of [parity](name:parity), this quantity retains only field orientation and takes the values $+1$ or $-1$; the two-valued indicator is undefined when the toroidal component vanishes. It does not specify field strength, plasma-current direction, or the even or odd symmetry of a gyrokinetic perturbation.

Sign convention: Positive when the toroidal magnetic-field component points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.
record.name: parity_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_at_flux_surface

record.documentation:
Electrical resistivity is the material property that determines the electric field required to sustain conduction in a mobile plasma-facing component unit. It governs induced-current and eddy-current response within that unit.

For an isotropic material, the local constitutive relation is

$$
\mathbf{E} = \rho\,\mathbf{J}
$$

where $\mathbf{E}$ is the local electric-field vector, $\rho$ is the electrical resistivity, and $\mathbf{J}$ is the conventional current-density vector.

This quantity applies to the material of one mobile plasma-facing component unit and is not summed over multiple units or converted into a lumped resistance. It is a local material property, distinct from the effective resistivity of a broader passive conducting structure or [wall material](name:resistivity_of_wall_material). When geometry is included, it contributes to a lumped [passive-loop resistance](name:resistance_of_passive_loop), which also depends on current-path length and cross-sectional geometry.

$$

$$

$$
I_{\mathrm{div}} = \int_{S_{\mathrm{div}}} \mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{ch}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}\, dA = \int_{S_{\mathrm{div}}} \sum_s q_s\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_s \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}\, dA
$$

where $I_{\mathrm{div}}$ is the total current in A, $S_{\mathrm{div}}$ is the union of divertor target surfaces, $\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{ch}}$ is conventional charged-particle current density in A m$^{-2}$, $q_s$ is the signed charge of species $s$ in C, $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_s$ is its particle flux density in m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$, and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ points from the plasma toward the material.

This assembly-integrated quantity differs from [current at a divertor target](name:current_at_divertor_target), which applies to one target, and [current of a divertor tile](name:current_of_divertor_tile), which applies to an individual tile.

Sign convention: Positive when conventional charged-particle current flows from the plasma into the divertor material.

record.documentation:
Alpha angle $\alpha$ specifies the inclination of the first cross-sectional axis at a coil conductor element. It applies to the oblique trapezoidal or parallelogram cross-sectional geometry of an active poloidal-field coil.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the angle is defined by

$$
\alpha = \operatorname{atan2}\!\left(\mathbf{a}_1\cdot\hat{Z},\,\mathbf{a}_1\cdot\hat{R}\right)
$$

where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The vector $\mathbf{a}_1$ points along the first cross-sectional axis; $\hat{R}$ and $\hat{Z}$ are the outward major-radius and upward unit vectors, respectively. The function $\operatorname{atan2}$ returns the quadrant-resolved angle from the radial and vertical projections.

This is an individual-element shape parameter, not an average over the coil. The [tilt angle of the coil conductor element](name:tilt_angle_of_coil_conductor_element) specifies the separate second inclination of the same cross-section.

Sign convention: Positive when the first cross-sectional axis rotates from the outward major-radius direction toward increasing vertical height.

record.documentation:

The global removal rate is defined by

$$
\Gamma_{e,\mathrm{pump}} = \frac{dN_{e,\mathrm{removed}}}{dt}
$$

where $\Gamma_{e,\mathrm{pump}}$ is the pumped particle-removal rate expressed in equivalent electrons, $N_{e,\mathrm{removed}}$ is the cumulative number of electron equivalents removed by wall pumping, and $t$ is time.

This quantity is aggregated over the wall and represents the total pumping throughput for the electron-equivalent population. The electron-equivalent basis does not assert that all removed particles are physical electrons, and the quantity is not an areal flux density, an electrical current, or a rate for one specified neutral species.

It is the electron-specific specialization of the general [particle-removal flux at the wall due to pumping](name:particle_rate_at_wall_due_to_pumping). In contrast, [neutral particle flux at the wall due to pumping](name:neutral_particle_flux_at_wall_due_to_pumping) uses a specified neutral species as its counting population rather than equivalent-electron counting.
record.name: electron_particle_flux_at_wall_due_to_pumping

$$

record.name: ethylene_source_rate

record.description: Dimensionless factor controlling the relative contribution of an interferometer beam’s line-integrated electron-density residual to an equilibrium objective function. At each equilibrium time slice, it is the nonnegative scalar w_i assigned to one such measurement constraint in J = (1/2) sum_i [w_i^2 (y_i^rec - y_i^meas)^2 / sigma_i^2], where y_i^rec and y_i^meas are the reconstructed and measured line-integrated electron densities, sigma_i is the standard deviation of the measurement error, and the sum runs over individual constraints. record.documentation:
The equilibrium weight assigned to an interferometer-beam constraint is a nonnegative factor that sets the relative importance of its line-integrated electron-density residual in an equilibrium objective function. It applies to the constraint associated with one interferometer beam rather than to the electron density itself.

A weighted least-squares objective containing this constraint is defined by

$$
J = \frac{1}{2} \sum_i w_i^2 \left(\frac{y_i^{\mathrm{rec}} - y_i^{\mathrm{meas}}}{\sigma_i}\right)^2
$$

where $J$ is the equilibrium objective function, $i$ indexes individual constraints, $w_i$ is the equilibrium weight, $y_i^{\mathrm{rec}}$ is the reconstructed line-integrated electron density for constraint $i$, $y_i^{\mathrm{meas}}$ is its measured line-integrated electron density, and $\sigma_i$ is the standard deviation assigned to its measurement error.

For this quantity, $i$ denotes an interferometer-beam line-integrated electron-density constraint. The weight is specific to that individual constraint; the objective function aggregates all constraint contributions through the summation. It is not the line-integrated electron density, either its measured or reconstructed value, and it is distinct from the [calibration coefficient of an interferometer beam](name:spectral_calibration_factor_at_line_of_sight), which characterizes signal calibration rather than equilibrium-objective weighting.

This quantity has the same objective-function role as the equilibrium weight of a flux loop and the equilibrium weight of a poloidal magnetic-field probe; those related weights differ by the physical measurement constraint to which they apply.

record.documentation:
Flux-surface-averaged magnetic-field magnitude is the mean strength of the total equilibrium [magnetic field](name:magnetic_field) on each closed nested magnetic flux surface.

Its defining relation is

$$
\langle B\rangle = \oint B\,dS/|\nabla\psi| \,/\, \oint dS/|\nabla\psi|
$$

where $B$ is the local total [magnetic-field magnitude](name:magnetic_field_magnitude), $\langle B\rangle$ is its flux-surface average, $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic-flux label, $\nabla\psi$ is the gradient of that label, and $dS$ is the area element of the closed surface over which both integrals are taken.

All equilibrium magnetic-field components contribute to the local magnitude before averaging. This quantity is not a selected field component, a pointwise field strength, or the magnitude of a surface-averaged field vector. It is positive for a nonvanishing equilibrium field.

The [flux-surface-averaged squared magnetic-field magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude) instead averages the square of the local field strength. That second moment is not the square of this mean unless the field strength is constant over the surface.

The flux-surface average is the average of a quantity over a closed magnetic flux surface, weighted by the inverse magnitude of the poloidal flux gradient.

The magnitude is the Euclidean norm of a vector quantity, or the modulus of a complex one.

record.description: Faraday angle is the signed rotation of a probing beam's linear-polarization orientation accumulated as the beam propagates through magnetized plasma. It is sensitive to the line integral of electron density times the magnetic-field component along the beam path and is used to constrain equilibrium reconstruction. It is a time-resolved scalar for one polarimeter channel (line of sight), evaluated relative to the beam's initial polarization orientation at its probing wavelength and expressed in rad. It may be measured directly or calculated from the reconstructed equilibrium at the selected time slice.
record.documentation:
Faraday angle is the signed rotation of the linear-polarization orientation of a probing electromagnetic wave induced by its passage through magnetized plasma. It is the variation of the polarization orientation accumulated between the beam's entry into and exit from the plasma.

In the cold, weakly dispersive magnetoionic limit, the plasma-induced rotation is approximated by

$$
\alpha = \frac{e^3\lambda^2}{8\pi^2\epsilon_0 m_e^2 c^3} \int_{\mathcal{L}} n_e(\ell) B_{\parallel}(\ell)\,d\ell
$$

where $\alpha$ is the Faraday angle, $e$ is the elementary-charge magnitude, $\lambda$ is the vacuum probing wavelength, $\pi$ is the circle constant, $\epsilon_0$ is the vacuum permittivity, $m_e$ is the electron mass, and $c$ is the speed of light. The path $\mathcal{L}$ is the segment of the probing beam crossing the plasma, $\ell$ is position along that path, $n_e(\ell)$ is the local [electron number density](name:electron_density), and $B_{\parallel}(\ell)$ is the signed magnetic-field component along the beam-propagation direction.

The quantity is the electron contribution accumulated along one probing-beam path through the plasma: its aggregation is a line integral along that path, not a local rotation rate, a flux-surface average, or an average or sum over beam paths. Rotation produced outside the plasma, including by optical or calibration elements, is excluded. The same physical angle may be realized either as a direct polarimetric observation or as the value calculated from a reconstructed equilibrium state along the same beam path; both denote this quantity, and their difference is a fit residual rather than another definition of it.

Faraday angle describes rotation of the polarization plane, whereas [polarization ellipticity of a polarimeter beam](name:polarization_ellipticity_of_polarimeter_beam) describes the shape of the polarization ellipse through its axis ratio; the two quantities are distinct and not interchangeable.

Sign convention: Positive when the polarization plane rotates according to the right-hand rule about the beam-propagation direction from its incident reference orientation.
record.name: faraday_angle

record.documentation:
The inverse square of total magnetic-field strength is a local magnetic-geometry factor that increases as the total field weakens and remains positive wherever the field magnitude is nonzero.

It is defined as the reciprocal of the [square of magnetic-field magnitude](name:square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude):

$$
B^{-2} = \frac{1}{B^2} = \frac{1}{\lvert \mathbf{B} \rvert^2}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is the total magnetic-field vector and $B$ is its magnitude.

The quantity applies to the full magnetic field in an equilibrium plasma, including all vector components and without restriction to a particle population. At the parent level it is a local quantity with no flux-surface or volume aggregation; it is distinct from the squared field magnitude itself and from the reciprocal square of any selected field component.

The [flux-surface-averaged inverse square of magnetic-field magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude) is obtained by applying a flux-surface average to this local factor. The averaging is a separate aggregation operation and does not alter the reciprocal-square transformation.
record.name: inverse_of_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude

record.documentation:
Loop voltage at plasma boundary

The voltage is defined by the electric-field circulation:

$$
V_{\mathrm{loop}} = \oint_C \mathbf{E}\cdot d\mathbf{l}
$$

where $V_{\mathrm{loop}}$ is the boundary loop voltage, $C$ is the closed toroidal loop at the plasma boundary, $\mathbf{E}$ is the electric field, and $d\mathbf{l}$ is the directed line element along the loop.

The total includes inductive contributions from both external sources and plasma currents. In contrast, [external loop voltage](name:external_loop_voltage) denotes only the contribution from changing externally generated linked magnetic flux. The inductive electric field provides the drive for [current due to ohmic current drive](name:current_due_to_ohmic_current_drive); the loop voltage is not an electrostatic potential difference between two points.

Sign convention: Positive when the electric-field circulation is directed along increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counterclockwise viewed from above) in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

The last closed magnetic flux surface: the outermost flux surface on which field lines close on themselves, bounding the confined plasma. Where $\psi = \psi_{\mathrm{LCFS}}$, $\psi$ is poloidal magnetic flux; $\psi_{\mathrm{LCFS}}$ is its value on the last closed flux surface.

record.documentation:
The lower-inner squareness of a flux surface is the dimensionless Luce (2013) shape coefficient that characterizes how the lower, high-field-side quadrant of a nested toroidal magnetic flux surface departs from a reference ellipse sharing the same center, horizontal half-width, and [elongation](name:elongation_of_flux_surface). It is the lower-quadrant component of [inner squareness of a flux surface](name:inner_squareness_of_flux_surface), complementary to [upper-inner squareness of a flux surface](name:upper_inner_squareness_of_flux_surface).

The reference ellipse is parameterized in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame by

$$
\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{ref}}(\theta)=\left(R_0+a\cos\theta,\;Z_0+\kappa a\sin\theta\right)
$$

where $R$ is major radius, $Z$ is vertical height, $\theta$ is a poloidal parameter, $(R_0,Z_0)$ is the ellipse center, $a$ is its horizontal half-width, and $\kappa$ is its elongation. Within the Luce model, $\zeta_{\mathrm{li}}=0$ represents no additional lower-inner corner shaping; positive values indicate an outward, boxier corner and negative values an inward, more indented corner.

This coefficient describes only the lower high-field-side quadrant and is not an average of the upper and lower inner coefficients.
record.name: lower_inner_squareness_of_flux_surface

$$
\ell_\beta = \left\lVert \mathbf{x}_{\beta,2} - \mathbf{x}_{\beta,1} \right\rVert
$$

where $\ell_\beta$ is the minor side length, $\mathbf{x}_{\beta,1}$ and $\mathbf{x}_{\beta,2}$ are the position vectors of its endpoints, and $\lVert\cdot\rVert$ denotes the Euclidean norm. The inclination angle $\beta$ is measured relative to the vertical height direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The quantity applies to one discrete plasma current-carrying filament element and is neither summed nor averaged over elements. It excludes the complementary major oblique side and therefore is distinct from [major length of the plasma filament](name:major_length_of_plasma_filament).

\rho_{\mathrm{minor}} = \frac{R_{\max}-R_{\min}}{2L_{\mathrm{ref}}}

record.description: Radial flux-surface location of the selected plasma boundary at a given equilibrium time slice, expressed by the normalized poloidal flux coordinate. It is the linear normalized poloidal flux value, increasing from zero at the magnetic axis to one at the separatrix, of the closed flux surface taken as the plasma boundary; fixed-boundary equilibrium calculations commonly set it slightly below one (typically 99.x%) to select a surface just inside the separatrix. record.documentation:
The normalized poloidal flux coordinate of the plasma boundary is the value of the [normalized poloidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate) on the closed flux surface selected as the plasma boundary. It is the linear normalized poloidal flux, labeling the boundary's radial position between the magnetic axis and the last closed flux surface.

Its value is the poloidal flux difference from the magnetic axis normalized to the axis-to-separatrix flux difference:

$$
\psi_{\mathrm{N}}^{\mathrm{boundary}} = \frac{\psi_{\mathrm{boundary}} - \psi_{\mathrm{axis}}}{\psi_{\mathrm{sep}} - \psi_{\mathrm{axis}}}
$$

where $\psi_{\mathrm{boundary}}$ is the [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) on the selected plasma-boundary surface, $\psi_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is the [poloidal magnetic flux at the magnetic axis](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis), and $\psi_{\mathrm{sep}}$ is the poloidal magnetic flux at the separatrix (last closed flux surface).

The label equals zero at the magnetic axis and equals one when the selected plasma boundary coincides with the separatrix; a value below one selects an internal closed flux surface. Its defining role is to specify, for fixed-boundary equilibrium representations, which closed flux surface is taken as the plasma boundary, commonly a surface just inside the separatrix so that the boundary remains strictly closed.

This is the linear normalized poloidal flux value itself, not its square root, and it is a flux-surface label rather than a signed poloidal-flux value or a geometric minor-radius measure. It is distinct from the toroidal-flux-based boundary label normalized toroidal flux coordinate at the plasma boundary, and it belongs to the same locus-valued family as the normalized poloidal flux coordinate at minimum safety factor and the [normalized poloidal flux coordinate of the pedestal](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_pedestal).

record.description: Particle energy is the energy associated with particle motion, inherited by specialized forms that are either a kinetic-energy-like coordinate of a velocity-space distribution or the kinetic energy of a particle population.
record.documentation:
Particle energy is the energy associated with the kinetic motion of particles. It is the general quantity inherited by its specialized forms, which differ in whether the energy is a coordinate attached to individual particle motion or a total carried by a particle population.

For a single particle of mass $m$ moving nonrelativistically with velocity $\mathbf{v}$, the underlying kinetic energy is:

$$
W = \frac{1}{2}m|\mathbf{v}|^2
$$

where $W$ is the particle kinetic energy, $m$ is the particle mass, and $\mathbf{v}$ is the particle velocity. Specialized forms use this energy, or an equivalent velocity-space weighting, in different roles.

The general quantity does not select a species, particle population, spatial region, velocity component, or aggregation convention. It is therefore not inherently a population-integrated total, not restricted to suprathermal particles, and not inherently a gyrokinetic coordinate. It is distinct from potential energy, thermal energy defined by a temperature, and field energy.

The specialized forms each fix part of this freedom. [Effective particle energy](name:effective_particle_energy) is a species-dependent, kinetic-energy-like coordinate that parameterizes a particle velocity-space distribution in gyrokinetic theory; it is a coordinate, not a population-integrated total. [Fast-particle energy](name:fast_particle_energy) is the total kinetic energy stored in a specified suprathermal population, integrated over the plasma volume and including motion parallel and perpendicular to the local magnetic field. The first fixes a species-dependent distribution coordinate, while the second fixes a population and a volume-integrated total.
record.name: particle_energy

It marks the external boundary of the conducting annular region. In the poloidal cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, it is the nonnegative distance r_outer = sqrt((R - R_c)^2 + (Z - Z_c)^2), where R is major radius, φ is toroidal angle, Z is vertical height, (R_c, Z_c) is the cross-section center, and (R, Z) is any point on the outer circular boundary. record.documentation:
Outer radius of a plasma filament is the geometric radius of the outer circular boundary of the annular cross-section representing a current-carrying plasma filament. It marks the external boundary of the conducting annular region; material outside this boundary is not part of that annular filament cross-section.

For the outer circular boundary in the poloidal cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the outer radius $r_\mathrm{outer}$ is the distance from the filament cross-section center $(R_c, Z_c)$ to any point $(R, Z)$ on that boundary:

$$
r_\mathrm{outer} = \sqrt{(R - R_c)^2 + (Z - Z_c)^2}
$$

where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, $Z$ is vertical height, $(R_c, Z_c)$ is the center of the annular cross-section, and $(R, Z)$ lies on the outer circular boundary.

The quantity applies only to the outer boundary of an annular plasma-filament cross-section and is a single geometric radius for that boundary, not an average over the conducting region. It is the outer member of radius of a plasma filament, paired with the [inner radius](name:inner_radius_of_plasma_filament) $r_\mathrm{inner}$; by definition $0 \le r_\mathrm{inner} \le r_\mathrm{outer}$, and the current-carrying cross-section occupies the annular region between the two radii. For the same annular geometry, the area of a plasma filament $A$ satisfies $A = \pi(r_\mathrm{outer}^2 - r_\mathrm{inner}^2)$, where $A$ is the area of the annular plasma-filament cross-section and $\pi$ is the circle constant. This quantity excludes the major radius of the filament center about the toroidal symmetry axis and rectangular cross-section dimensions such as [plasma filament width](name:plasma_filament_width) and [height of a plasma filament](name:height_of_plasma_filament).
record.name: outer_radius_of_plasma_filament

record.description: Poloidal beta compares volume-averaged plasma pressure with an effective poloidal magnetic-pressure scale set by net plasma current and plasma geometry. It is defined as βp = 4∫_V p dV/(R₀μ₀Ip²), with dimensionless unit 1, where p is the pressure supplied by the plasma or equilibrium representation, R₀ is the reference major radius, μ₀ is vacuum permeability and Ip is the plasma current used by that normalization. record.documentation: Poloidal beta compares the volume-averaged plasma pressure with a current-based poloidal magnetic-pressure scale. Its source normalization is $\beta_p=4\int_V p\,dV/(R_0\mu_0 I_p^2)$. Here $p$ is the pressure supplied by the plasma or equilibrium representation, $V$ is the evaluation volume, $R_0$ is the reference major radius, $\mu_0$ is vacuum permeability and $I_p$ is the plasma current used by that normalization. The global value uses the plasma volume; a radial profile uses the volume inside each flux surface as a function of poloidal flux. Equilibrium values are evaluated at each time slice; the equilibrium-reconstruction estimate uses pressure determined by an equilibrium reconstruction code. Writing $\langle p\rangle_V=V^{-1}\int_Vp\,dV$, the same quantity obeys the canonical beta relation $$\beta = \frac{2\mu_0 \langle p\rangle}{B^2}$$ with $\beta=\beta_p$, $\langle p\rangle=\langle p\rangle_V$ and $B=B_{p,\mathrm{ref}}$. The effective reference field satisfies $B_{p,\mathrm{ref}}^2=\frac{\mu_0^2I_p^2R_0}{2V}$. The reference field is an effective current-based scale rather than a pointwise poloidal field. The normalization requires nonzero $I_p$ and positive evaluation volume. It is neither an average of local pressure-to-field ratios nor an unnormalized pressure. Unlike [toroidal beta](name:toroidal_beta), it uses the current-based poloidal scale.

record.documentation:
This quantity is the geometric area enclosed by the last closed magnetic flux surface (LCFS), which forms the plasma boundary, in a poloidal cross-section.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, the enclosed area is defined by

$$
A_{\rm LCFS} = \iint_{\mathcal{S}_{\rm LCFS}} dR\,dZ
$$

where $A_{\rm LCFS}$ is the LCFS cross-sectional area, $\mathcal{S}_{\rm LCFS}$ is the region enclosed by the LCFS contour at fixed toroidal angle $\phi$, $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, $Z$ is vertical height, and $dR\,dZ$ is the poloidal-plane area element.

This is a global equilibrium quantity for the complete plasma-boundary contour. It is not a local surface element, a flux-surface average, or the area of a toroidal surface formed by revolving the contour.

It is the plasma-boundary specialization of [poloidal plane cross-sectional area of a flux surface](name:poloidal_plane_cross_sectional_area_of_flux_surface), whose corresponding area is defined for an arbitrary closed magnetic flux surface; the LCFS is the outermost such surface enclosing the plasma.

record.documentation:
The poloidal length is the perimeter of the closed contour formed by one selected magnetic flux surface in a poloidal cross-section. It is a geometric property of the surface boundary, rather than its enclosed area, volume, or toroidal circumference.

The contour length is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height:

$$
L_{\mathrm{pol}} = \int_{\theta_a}^{\theta_b} \sqrt{\left(\frac{dR(\theta)}{d\theta}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{dZ(\theta)}{d\theta}\right)^2}\,d\theta
$$

Here $L_{\mathrm{pol}}$ is the poloidal length, $\theta$ is any smooth parameter along the contour, $R(\theta)$ and $Z(\theta)$ are its cylindrical coordinate functions, and $\theta_a$ and $\theta_b$ are parameter values at the same contour point after one complete circuit. The contour is taken at fixed toroidal angle $\phi$.

The quantity applies to one magnetic flux surface and includes the complete closed poloidal contour, with no averaging or summation over multiple surfaces. It excludes local arc segments and geometric quantities associated with the enclosed region. The selected surface may be labeled by the [normalized poloidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate).

Unlike [elongation of a flux surface](name:elongation_of_flux_surface), which describes a scale-independent cross-sectional shape ratio, the poloidal length retains the absolute geometric scale of the contour.

record.documentation:
Poloidal magnetic flux is the net magnetic flux through a horizontal disk centered on the toroidal symmetry axis and bounded by the toroidal circle through the evaluation point. It specializes [magnetic flux](name:magnetic_flux) by specifying the integration surface and its orientation. In axisymmetric equilibrium, its level sets define magnetic surfaces.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle increasing counterclockwise when viewed from above, and $Z$ is vertical height. The full poloidal magnetic flux is defined by

$$
\Phi_{\mathrm{p}}(R,Z) \equiv \psi(R,Z) = 2\pi \int_0^R B_Z(R',Z)\,R'\,dR'
$$

where $\Phi_{\mathrm{p}}$, also denoted $\psi$, is the poloidal magnetic flux, $B_Z$ is the vertical magnetic-field component, and $R'$ is the radial integration variable. The factor $2\pi$ accounts for integration around the complete toroidal circle.

This quantity includes contributions from plasma currents and external sources, unlike [external magnetic flux](name:external_magnetic_flux), which excludes the plasma-generated contribution. It is the full flux, not flux divided by $2\pi$, a normalized coordinate, or a cross-sectional average. It differs from [toroidal magnetic flux](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux), which integrates the toroidal magnetic field through a poloidal cross-section.

The [magnetic-axis value](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis) and [plasma-boundary value](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary) are evaluations of this same function and provide the endpoint references for poloidal-flux normalization. For nested surfaces enclosing positive toroidal plasma current flowing toward increasing $\phi$, the poloidal flux decreases from the magnetic axis to the plasma boundary.

Sign convention: Positive when the magnetic field threading the horizontal disk has a net component toward increasing $Z$, along the upward surface normal.
record.name: poloidal_magnetic_flux

record.description: Poloidal magnetic flux at the magnetic axis is the signed equilibrium flux through a horizontal disk centered on the toroidal symmetry axis and bounded by the toroidal circle at that location. Its sign is positive when the net vertical magnetic field threading the disk is directed toward increasing Z. It is a zero-dimensional scalar at each time slice and may be represented as a one-dimensional function of time. Together with the plasma-boundary flux Φ_p,b, it supplies the axis reference for the normalization (Φ_p − Φ_p,a)/(Φ_p,b − Φ_p,a), provided the reference values differ, even when the radial grid does not extend to the axis or boundary. record.documentation:
Poloidal magnetic flux at the magnetic axis is the signed [magnetic flux](name:magnetic_flux) through a horizontal disk centered on the toroidal symmetry axis and bounded by the toroidal circle at that location. It is the magnetic-axis value of the equilibrium [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) function.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, its defining relation is

$$
\Phi_{\mathrm{p},a} = \Phi_{\mathrm{p}}(R_a,Z_a) = 2\pi \int_0^{R_a} B_Z(R',Z_a)\,R'\,dR'
$$

where $\Phi_{\mathrm{p},a}$ is the magnetic-axis poloidal flux, $\Phi_{\mathrm{p}}$ is the equilibrium poloidal magnetic-flux function, $R_a$ and $Z_a$ are the magnetic-axis coordinates, $R'$ is the major-radius integration variable, and $B_Z$ is the vertical magnetic-field component.

This value includes both externally generated and plasma-current-generated flux; it is not an external-source-only contribution. It is an unnormalized flux value and need not vanish at the magnetic axis.

Together with the [poloidal magnetic flux at the plasma boundary](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary), denoted by $\Phi_{\mathrm{p},b}$, it defines the normalized poloidal-flux coordinate $\Phi_{\mathrm{p},N} = (\Phi_{\mathrm{p}}-\Phi_{\mathrm{p},a})/(\Phi_{\mathrm{p},b}-\Phi_{\mathrm{p},a})$. This coordinate is zero at the magnetic axis and one at the plasma boundary, provided the two reference flux values differ. These physical reference endpoints apply even when the flux-coordinate interval under consideration does not extend to the axis or boundary.

Sign convention: Positive when the net vertical magnetic field threading the integration disk is directed toward increasing $Z$.

The closed magnetic-field line about which nested toroidal magnetic flux surfaces are arranged. Where $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{p}}(R_{\mathrm{axis}}, Z_{\mathrm{axis}}) = 0$, $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{p}}$ is poloidal magnetic field; $R_{\mathrm{axis}}, Z_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is the O-point inside the nested closed flux surfaces.

record.description: Major-radius coordinate of the plasma-current centroid in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame at each equilibrium time slice, obtained by normalizing the toroidal-current first moment over the poloidal plasma cross-section by total plasma current, expressed in m.
record.documentation:
The radial coordinate of the current center is the major-radius location of the centroid of the toroidal plasma-current distribution. It identifies a current-weighted position and is distinct from the geometric centroid or the magnetic axis.

The coordinate is defined by the toroidal-current first moment:

$$
R_c = \frac{\displaystyle\int_{D_p} R\,j_\phi\,dS}{I_p}
$$

where $R_c$ is the major-radius coordinate of the current center, $R$ is the major-radius coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $j_\phi$ is the toroidal component of the plasma [current density](name:current_density), $dS$ is an element of poloidal cross-sectional area, $D_p$ is the plasma current-carrying poloidal cross-section, and $I_p$ is the total toroidal plasma current, equal to the corresponding integral of $j_\phi$ over $D_p$.

The quantity applies to the full plasma-current distribution and uses a current-weighted first-moment aggregation over the poloidal cross-section. It excludes weighting by particle density, pressure, magnetic-field strength, or geometric area alone; the resulting position is therefore not a generic geometric center.

This quantity is a locus-specific instance of the general [radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate), evaluated at the current center. Its vertical counterpart, [vertical coordinate of the current center](name:vertical_coordinate_of_current_center), supplies the corresponding vertical position needed to locate the current centroid in the cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.
record.name: radial_coordinate_of_current_center

It is the minimum major radius on that surface, R_in(S) = min_{x in S} R(x), with R_in(S) < R_axis, where R_axis is the major radius of the magnetic axis. record.documentation:
This quantity is the major-radius coordinate of the point where a magnetic flux surface intersects the inboard midplane, identifying the high-field-side location of that surface relative to the toroidal symmetry axis. It is a locus-specific form of the [radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate).

For a magnetic flux surface $\mathcal{S}$, the inboard-midplane radial coordinate is defined by

$$
R_{\mathrm{in}}(\mathcal{S}) = R\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{in}}(\mathcal{S})\right)
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{in}}(\mathcal{S})$ is the quantity defined here, $R(\mathbf{x})$ is the major-radius coordinate of spatial position $\mathbf{x}$, $\mathcal{S}$ is the specified magnetic flux surface, and $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{in}}(\mathcal{S})$ is its inboard midplane intersection. The coordinates are expressed in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The scope is one coordinate value for each specified magnetic flux surface at its inboard, high-field-side midplane intersection. It is not a flux-surface average, a poloidal or toroidal average, or the corresponding outboard-midplane coordinate; the latter is represented by [radial coordinate at outboard midplane](name:radial_coordinate_at_outboard_midplane). Unlike [radial magnetic field](name:radial_magnetic_field), this quantity describes the location of a surface and not a magnetic-field component.

This quantity specializes [radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate) by fixing the evaluation locus to the inboard midplane. Comparing it with the outboard-midplane value characterizes the horizontal extent and radial placement of the same magnetic flux surface.
record.name: radial_coordinate_at_inboard_midplane

record.description: Total power deposited on a divertor target by recombination processes, summing the plasma-ion and neutral-particle recombination channels at the plasma-material interface. The power refers to a single divertor target, is non-negative, is inferred from edge plasma simulations or from particle flux measurements combined with surface energy-release models, and is expressed in W.
record.documentation:
This quantity captures the combined recombination power delivered to a single divertor target, encompassing two physically distinct contributions: energy released when plasma ions recombine at or near the target surface (the plasma channel, quantified by plasma_power_at_divertor_target_due_to_recombination) and energy deposited when neutral particles undergo recombination into lower-energy bound states at the material wall (the neutral channel, quantified by [neutral_power_at_divertor_target_due_to_recombination](name:neutral_power_at_divertor_target_due_to_recombination)).

The total recombination power at the target decomposes additively:

$$
P_{\rm rec,target} = P_{\rm rec,plasma} + P_{\rm rec,neutral}
$$

where $P_{\rm rec,plasma}$ is the ion-recombination contribution and $P_{\rm rec,neutral}$ is the neutral-particle recombination contribution, both in W.

This target-localized quantity is a spatial specialization of [power_due_to_recombination](name:power_due_to_recombination), which encompasses recombination power deposited on plasma-facing materials without restriction to a particular surface location. In attached divertor operation, recombination power at the target is a minor fraction of the total heat load; in detached or high-recycling regimes, surface and volumetric recombination become significant energy sinks that reduce the conducted and convected flux reaching the target. It is inferred from edge plasma simulations or from particle flux measurements combined with surface energy-release models, and is non-negative by definition.
record.name: power_at_divertor_target_due_to_recombination

record.documentation:
Ratio of the squared toroidal-flux-coordinate gradient magnitude to squared major radius is a local equilibrium metric coefficient. It encodes flux-surface spacing with inverse-square major-radius weighting.

The defining relation is:

$$
G = \frac{|\nabla \rho_{\mathrm{tor}}|^2}{R^2}
$$

where $G$ is this local coefficient, $\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the length-valued toroidal-flux coordinate, and $\nabla$ is the spatial gradient operator. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $R$ is the distance from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle, and $Z$ is the vertical height.

The toroidal-flux coordinate retains its prescribed scale; no boundary normalization or substitution of an arbitrary flux label is implied. The denominator is squared major radius, not its inverse. The squared gradient magnitude distinguishes this coefficient from inverse squared major radius alone.

This quantity is a pointwise ratio without spatial averaging. Its flux-surface-averaged counterpart averages the complete ratio over a closed magnetic flux surface; it is not the ratio of separately averaged numerator and denominator.

record.description: Plasma current is the total signed conventional electric current carried toroidally by the entire plasma population through a complete poloidal cross-section; for a Fiber Optic Current Sensor (FOCS) measurement, the integration region is the area outlined by the FOCS fibre path on the vacuum vessel. It is obtained by integrating the toroidal projection of plasma current density over the specified area, at fixed toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, with positive normal in the direction of increasing phi. Positive current is counterclockwise when viewed from above +Z. The unit is A. Values may be measured, computed from magnetic measurements, derived from profiles, or calculated from a reconstructed MHD equilibrium; FOCS measurements use the Faraday magneto-optic effect and are time-resolved. During plasma initiation, the quantity tracks current buildup from breakdown through early ramp-up before a full MHD equilibrium is established. Each value is scalar; bound representations have zero or one array dimension, and the magnetics method array has coordinate 1...N, with the generally recommended calculation method first. Related specialized quantities retain the signed-current meaning while restricting the population, selecting a current direction, or limiting the enclosed region.
record.documentation:
Plasma current is the net conventional electric current carried in the toroidal direction by the entire plasma population. It is the signed total through a complete poloidal cross-section, or through the area outlined by the FOCS for a FOCS measurement, with contributions in opposite directions combined algebraically.

The total plasma current is the toroidal projection of plasma current density integrated over the full plasma cross-section:

$$
I_p = \int_{A_p} \mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{pl}} \cdot \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}\,\mathrm{d}A
$$

where $I_p$ is plasma current, $A_p$ is the full poloidal cross-sectional area occupied by the plasma, $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{pl}}$ is the total plasma [current density](name:current_density), $\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$ is the toroidal unit vector, and $\mathrm{d}A$ is a differential cross-sectional area element. The cross-section is at fixed toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; its positive normal is $+\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$. For a FOCS measurement, the integration region is instead the area outlined by the FOCS fibre path on the vacuum vessel; it recovers the full plasma total when that area encloses the complete plasma cross-section.

The total includes current contributions from all plasma charge carriers over the complete cross-section; it is neither a species-resolved current nor an unsigned particle flow or current-density magnitude. Currents carried by external coils and [passive structures](name:current_of_passive_structure) are excluded. Related specialized plasma-current quantities retain the signed conventional-current meaning while specifying a restricted population, direction, or region.

The [cumulative plasma current inside a magnetic flux surface](name:cumulative_inside_flux_surface_plasma_current) restricts the integrated region to the area enclosed by that surface; its toroidal value at the full plasma boundary recovers this total. The [parallel cumulative plasma current inside a flux surface](name:parallel_cumulative_inside_flux_surface_plasma_current) instead selects the local magnetic-field direction, so it is not generally equal to the toroidal current. The [total toroidal runaway-electron current](name:toroidal_total_runaway_electron_current) is the contribution from the runaway-electron population, not the total current of the plasma.

Sign convention: Positive when conventional plasma current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counterclockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$).
record.name: plasma_current

record.documentation:
This quantity is the signed major-radius offset between a measurement position mapped along its magnetic flux surface to the outboard midplane and the separatrix at that locus.

The defining relation is

$$
\Delta R_{\mathrm{sep,mid}} = R_{\mathrm{mapped}} - R_{\mathrm{sep,mid}}
$$

where $\Delta R_{\mathrm{sep,mid}}$ is the signed separation, $R_{\mathrm{mapped}}$ is the major radius of the mapped measurement position, and $R_{\mathrm{sep,mid}}$ is the major radius of the separatrix intersection at the outboard midplane. Both radii are coordinates in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is distance from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The mapping preserves the magnetic flux label of the original measurement position. The result is a difference of major radii, not the [radial coordinate assigned to a flux surface](name:radial_coordinate_of_flux_surface), an unmapped local separation, or the shortest distance normal to the separatrix. It vanishes on the separatrix and is negative on the confined-plasma side.

Sign convention: Positive when the mapped measurement position has a larger major radius than the separatrix at the outboard midplane, corresponding to the scrape-off-layer side.

The low-field-side equatorial midplane: the point of maximum major radius on the flux surface in question. For a value at the separatrix intersection use outboard_midplane_separatrix. Where $R = \max_{S} R,\quad R > R_{\mathrm{axis}}$, $S$ is the magnetic flux surface the point lies on; $R_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is major radius of the magnetic axis.
