record.description: Real part of the first-order radial magnetic-vector-potential eigenfunction for a single toroidal mode in the vacuum region, from linear MHD stability analysis. The quantity is provided for each time slice as a two-dimensional array, in T.m. The radial projection is taken toward increasing major radius R in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, and the real part is defined relative to the phase reference of the complex eigenfunction.
record.documentation:
The quantity is the real radial projection of the first-order perturbed magnetic vector-potential eigenfunction in the vacuum region for one toroidal Fourier mode. The real part is defined relative to the phase reference of that complex eigenfunction.

$$
A_{R,\mathrm{vac}}^{\mathrm{Re}} = \operatorname{Re}\!\left(\widetilde{\mathbf{A}}_{\mathrm{vac}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{R}}\right)
$$

Here $A_{R,\mathrm{vac}}^{\mathrm{Re}}$ is the requested real radial component, $\widetilde{\mathbf{A}}_{\mathrm{vac}}$ is the complex first-order perturbed magnetic vector-potential eigenfunction in the vacuum region, $\hat{\mathbf{R}}$ is the radial unit vector, and $\operatorname{Re}$ denotes the real-part operation. The radial direction is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The quantity applies outside the plasma and to one toroidal Fourier mode; it is not summed over modes. It excludes the plasma-region perturbation, the imaginary component, and the unreduced complex radial component. The [radial perturbed vacuum magnetic vector potential](name:radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential) is the full complex parent quantity, of which this entry is the real-part component. It is distinct from the [radial perturbed vacuum magnetic field](name:radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field), which is a magnetic-field perturbation rather than a vector potential.

Sign convention: Positive when the real radial projection points toward increasing major radius $R$.
record.name: radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential_real_part

record.description: Second local tangential width of the optical element is the full clear-aperture extent between opposing edges of its rectangular opening along the second object-local tangential axis.
record.documentation:
Width of optical element

The width is defined by the difference between opposing aperture-edge coordinates:

$$
w = X_{2,\max} - X_{2,\min}
$$

where $w$ is the full aperture width, and $X_{2,\max}$ and $X_{2,\min}$ are the maximum and minimum aperture-edge coordinates along the second local tangential axis. In the object-local aperture-plane coordinates $(X_1, X_2)$, $X_1$ and $X_2$ denote positions along the first and second local tangential axes, respectively.

This non-negative quantity applies only to rectangular aperture geometry and denotes the full width, not the half-width. It describes the usable clear opening, excluding opaque mounts and structures outside the aperture. The orthogonal aperture dimension is the [first local tangential width of the optical element](name:first_local_tangential_width_of_optical_element), measured along $X_1$.

record.description: Spectral photon radiance is the directional photon arrival rate from plasma emission per projected area, viewing solid angle, and wavelength interval.
record.documentation:
Spectral photon radiance describes the absolute photon-number brightness of plasma radiation along a specified viewing direction, resolved by wavelength. Its spectral dependence is expressed per wavelength interval, not per frequency or photon-energy interval.

The defining differential relation is:

$$
dN_{\gamma} = L_{\gamma}(\lambda)\,dt\,dA_{\perp}\,d\Omega\,d\lambda
$$

where $N_{\gamma}$ is the number of photons crossing a collecting surface, $L_{\gamma}(\lambda)$ is the spectral photon radiance at wavelength $\lambda$, $t$ is time, $A_{\perp}$ is the collecting surface's projected area perpendicular to the ray direction, and $\Omega$ is the solid angle about that direction.

The quantity includes the line and continuum contributions present at the specified wavelength without selecting a particular emitting species or radiation mechanism. It is not a local volumetric photon-production rate, an electromagnetic energy radiance, or a detector count rate.

Integrating the contribution from an identified transition over its wavelength interval gives the [photon radiance at a spectral line](name:photon_radiance_at_spectral_line), rather than a wavelength-resolved radiance density. The [spectral bremsstrahlung photon radiance](name:spectral_bremsstrahlung_photon_radiance) is the contribution restricted to free-free emission.
record.name: spectral_photon_radiance

record.description: Full thickness of a rectangular plasma filament cross-section, measured along the in-plane direction normal to the filament's central segment. It is the transverse side length of the rectangle, complementing the tangential length measured along the segment. The local plane is a poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The thickness is a non-negative length in m.
record.documentation:
Thickness of a plasma filament is the full transverse extent of a rectangular (thick-line) filament cross-section, measured in the local plane of the element along the direction normal to the filament's central segment. The central segment lies in a poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, and the local tangential-normal basis is defined within that plane: the tangential direction follows the central segment while the normal direction is the in-plane perpendicular. It is a full side length, not a half-width.

For a rectangular filament cross-section, the cross-sectional area is the product of the two full local side lengths:

$$
A_\mathrm{fil} = L_\mathrm{tan}\, t
$$

where $A_\mathrm{fil}$ is the filament cross-sectional area in $\mathrm{m}^2$, $L_\mathrm{tan}$ is the tangential length in $\mathrm{m}$, and $t$ is the thickness in $\mathrm{m}$. When the local tangential and normal directions align with the cylindrical axes, the thickness coincides with either the width (radial $R$-direction extent) or the [height](name:height_of_plasma_filament) (vertical $Z$-direction extent) of the same rectangular cross-section.

In equilibrium filament descriptions, the thickness is set by the chosen local geometric representation of a discrete current-carrying plasma element. For a thick-line element it is specified directly as the rectangle side perpendicular to the central segment.

The value is a non-negative geometric length governed by the spatial resolution and local size of the filament representation. No universal device-independent numerical range applies; it should be interpreted relative to the associated tangential length and to neighboring filament spacing.
record.name: thickness_of_plasma_filament

record.description: Safety factor at the magnetic axis is the limiting signed number of toroidal field-line turns per poloidal circuit as neighboring closed flux surfaces approach the axis. In axisymmetry, or using straight-field-line flux coordinates (ρ, θ, φ), it is q₀ = lim_{ρ→0} q(ρ), where q(ρ) = (1/(2π)) ∮ (B·∇φ)/(B·∇θ) dθ, integrated over one complete poloidal circuit, and ρ is a monotonic flux-surface label vanishing at the magnetic axis. Here B is the magnetic field, ∇ is the spatial gradient operator, θ is the poloidal angle, and φ is the toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, with R the major radius, Z the vertical height, and increasing φ counterclockwise when viewed from above. The value is positive when the field-line toroidal advance is toward increasing φ as θ increases. It is evaluated by the neighboring-surface limit, not by direct evaluation of the poloidal-angle integral at the axis, and is neither a spatial average nor a sum. It is a dimensionless scalar, with unit 1, at each equilibrium time slice; the summary source represents its values in a one-dimensional array.
record.documentation:
Safety factor at magnetic axis

In axisymmetry, or using straight-field-line flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, the neighboring-surface [safety factor](name:safety_factor) is defined by

$$
q = \frac{1}{2\pi}\oint \frac{\mathbf{B}\cdot\nabla\phi}{\mathbf{B}\cdot\nabla\theta}\,d\theta
$$

where $q$ is the signed safety factor, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field, $\nabla$ is the spatial gradient operator, $\rho$ is a monotonic flux-surface label vanishing at the magnetic axis, $\theta$ is the poloidal angle, and $\phi$ is the toroidal angle. The integral covers one complete poloidal circuit. The toroidal angle belongs to the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height; increasing $\phi$ is counterclockwise when viewed from above.

The axis value $q_0$ is defined by the limit $q_0 = \lim_{\rho\to0}q(\rho)$, rather than by direct evaluation of the poloidal-angle integral at the axis. It is a locus-specific value, not a spatial average or a sum. It is also distinct from the [minimum safety factor](name:minimum_safety_factor), which selects the signed value where the winding magnitude is smallest and need not occur at the magnetic axis.

Sign convention: Positive when the toroidal angle advance of a magnetic field line is in the direction of increasing $\phi$ as the poloidal angle $\theta$ increases.

The closed magnetic-field line about which nested toroidal magnetic flux surfaces are arranged. Where $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{p}}(R_{\mathrm{axis}}, Z_{\mathrm{axis}}) = 0$, $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{p}}$ is poloidal magnetic field; $R_{\mathrm{axis}}, Z_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is the O-point inside the nested closed flux surfaces.
record.name: safety_factor_at_magnetic_axis

record.description: Toroidal angle locating each point of a control surface about the machine symmetry axis, measured in the right-handed cylindrical frame from the facility-defined zero direction. At each time slice, the angles form a one-dimensional array indexed from 1 to N on which the Fourier decomposition of the normal components of the magnetic field is carried out. The unit is rad.
record.documentation:
The toroidal angle identifies the azimuthal location of a point on the control surface about the machine symmetry axis. It is the geometrical coordinate defined for [toroidal angle](name:toroidal_angle), with the control-surface locus providing the points to which it applies.

For a point with Cartesian coordinates $x$ and $y$ in the right-handed $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ basis, the angle in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame is defined by:

$$
\phi = \operatorname{atan2}(y,x) \pmod{2\pi}
$$

where $R$ is the major radius, $Z$ is vertical height, and the zero of $\phi$ follows the facility-defined reference direction. The angle is periodic, so values differing by an integer multiple of $2\pi$ represent the same toroidal direction; it is distinct from the vertical coordinate of the control surface.

Sign convention: Positive when $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above the $+\hat{Z}$ direction.
record.name: toroidal_angle_of_control_surface

record.description: Complex scalar E-minus coefficient of a coherent electromagnetic-wave electric field, transverse to the static magnetic field and retaining the amplitude and phase of its right-hand circular polarization. It is obtained as the circular-basis projection Ẽ₋ = e₋* · Ẽ_wave, with the unit-normalized basis vector e₋ = (ê₁ − iê₂)/√2 in a local right-handed orthonormal frame (ê₁, ê₂, b̂), where b̂ points along the static magnetic field. With temporal dependence exp(−iωt), this component co-rotates with positive-ion gyromotion and drives ion cyclotron resonance heating (ICRH); handedness is relative to the static magnetic field, not the wave-propagation direction. For each frequency and time slice of the full-wave solution, one scalar value is provided per element of a generic-grid-description grid subset, stored as a one-dimensional array indexed from 1 to N. The unit is V.m^-1.
record.documentation: The right-hand circularly polarized wave electric field is the E-minus polarization coefficient of the complex [wave electric field](name:wave_electric_field), perpendicular to the local static magnetic field. It retains the local amplitude and phase of that circular-polarization contribution. Its scalar coefficient is defined by the circular-basis projection $\widetilde E_{-}=\mathbf e_{-}^{*}\cdot\widetilde{\mathbf E}_{\mathrm{wave}}$, where $\widetilde E_{-}$ is the right-hand circularly polarized complex coefficient, $\widetilde{\mathbf E}_{\mathrm{wave}}$ is the wave-electric-field phasor, and the asterisk denotes complex conjugation. The circular basis vector is $\mathbf e_{-}=(\hat{\mathbf e}_1-i\hat{\mathbf e}_2)/\sqrt{2}$, where $i$ is the imaginary unit. The real unit vectors form a local right-handed orthonormal frame $(\hat{\mathbf e}_1,\hat{\mathbf e}_2,\hat{\mathbf b})$, with $\hat{\mathbf b}$ pointing along the static magnetic field and the first two directions perpendicular to it. With temporal dependence $e^{-i\omega t}$, where $\omega$ is the wave angular frequency and $t$ is time, this polarization co-rotates with positive-ion gyromotion. This component drives ion cyclotron resonance heating (ICRH) and is key to wave-particle coupling. The complementary [left-hand circularly polarized wave electric field](name:left_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field) rotates opposite to positive-ion gyromotion under this convention. Handedness is defined relative to the static magnetic field, not the wave-propagation direction. This quantity includes only the right-hand transverse wave contribution; it excludes the parallel wave component and non-wave electric fields. It is local and is not restricted to a beam or ray path. For each frequency and time slice of the full-wave solution, one scalar value is provided per element of a generic-grid-description grid subset, stored as a one-dimensional array indexed from 1 to N. The full complex coefficient is distinct from its amplitude representation, which removes the coefficient's complex phase, and from its real and [imaginary quadratures](name:right_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_imaginary_part), which separately retain phase-referenced parts of the same phasor.
record.name: right_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field

record.description: Toroidal magnetic field at the magnetic axis is the signed component of the total equilibrium magnetic field in the toroidal direction, including external-coil and plasma-current contributions. It is computed from the equilibrium reconstruction as the local projection B_axis · φ̂ in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, positive in the direction of increasing toroidal angle, counterclockwise when viewed from above. The magnetic axis is the closed magnetic-field line about which nested toroidal magnetic flux surfaces are arranged, located at the poloidal-field O-point where B_p = 0. The value is neither a magnetic-field magnitude nor a flux-surface average. It is a scalar at each equilibrium time slice; the summary representations are one-dimensional arrays of local values. record.documentation:
Toroidal magnetic field at the magnetic axis is the signed toroidal projection of the total equilibrium [magnetic field](name:magnetic_field). It is evaluated locally at the magnetic axis.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, the defining projection is:

$$
B_{\phi,\mathrm{axis}} = \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{axis}} \cdot \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}
$$

where $B_{\phi,\mathrm{axis}}$ is the toroidal magnetic field at the magnetic axis, $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is the total equilibrium magnetic-field vector at that locus, and $\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle.

The total field includes externally applied and plasma-current-generated contributions. The corresponding projection of the [vacuum magnetic field](name:vacuum_magnetic_field) excludes plasma-current contributions and is therefore a distinct quantity. This on-axis value is neither a magnetic-field magnitude nor a flux-surface average.

Sign convention: Positive when the magnetic field at the magnetic axis projects in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, counterclockwise when viewed from above.

The closed magnetic-field line about which nested toroidal magnetic flux surfaces are arranged. Where $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{p}}(R_{\mathrm{axis}}, Z_{\mathrm{axis}}) = 0$, $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{p}}$ is poloidal magnetic field; $R_{\mathrm{axis}}, Z_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is the O-point inside the nested closed flux surfaces.

record.description: Signed azimuthal orientation angle of a poloidal magnetic-field probe’s sensitive-axis normal in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, obtained from its horizontal projection with opposite projected normals folded into the same principal orientation, and expressed in radians. The angle is zero for an orientation fully in the poloidal plane.
record.documentation:
This quantity is the signed toroidal orientation of the sensitive-axis normal of a poloidal magnetic-field probe coil. It measures the normal’s departure from the poloidal plane through the orientation of its horizontal projection, with opposite projected normals identified.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, the angle is defined by

$$
\alpha_{\mathrm{tor}} = \tfrac{1}{2}\operatorname{atan2}(2n_Rn_\phi,n_R^2-n_\phi^2), \qquad n_R=\mathbf{n}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{R}}, \quad n_\phi=\mathbf{n}\cdot\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}
$$

where $\alpha_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the toroidal orientation angle, $\mathbf{n}$ is the probe’s sensitive-axis unit normal, $n_R$ and $n_\phi$ are its cylindrical radial and toroidal components, and $\hat{\mathbf{R}}$ and $\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$ are the radial and toroidal unit vectors. Here $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; the half-angle expression returns the signed principal orientation from the radial direction to the horizontal projection of $\mathbf{n}$, with opposite projected normals folded into the same orientation.

The quantity applies to the geometric orientation of each poloidal magnetic-field probe coil. It is not the local plasma magnetic field, a field component, or an angle averaged over probes, turns, or field samples. The angle determines how the probe’s sensitive direction is related to the local magnetic-field vector and therefore how the measured component is projected. The corresponding toroidal orientation for a toroidal probe is defined by [toroidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe](name:toroidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe), while its independent poloidal tilt is represented by [poloidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe](name:poloidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe).

Sign convention: Positive when rotation from the positive radial direction toward the folded horizontal projection of the sensitive-axis normal is toward increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.
record.name: toroidal_angle_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe

record.description: Number density of tungsten ions summed over all positive ionization states, excluding neutral tungsten, at a specified location or spatial average.
record.documentation:
Tungsten-ion number density is the particle count per unit volume for all positively charged tungsten ions, with neutral tungsten excluded. It may denote a local value or a spatially averaged value over a defined domain.

The charge-state-summed density is defined by

$$
n_{\mathrm{W}} = \sum_{Z=1}^{74} n_{\mathrm{W}}^{Z+}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{W}}$ and $n_{\mathrm{W}}^{Z+}$ are number densities in m$^{-3}$, and $Z$ is the positive tungsten charge state. Specific instances include [volume-averaged tungsten density](name:volume_averaged_tungsten_density), [tungsten density at magnetic axis](name:tungsten_density_at_magnetic_axis), and [tungsten density at divertor target](name:tungsten_density_at_divertor_target); these differ by evaluation locus or averaging domain. Neutral tungsten is not included.
record.name: tungsten_density

record.description: Toroidal total current density is the net conventional charge flux per unit area around the symmetry axis, formed by algebraically summing all included current contributions. It is the signed local projection onto increasing toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, where R is major radius and Z is vertical height, and is measured in A.m^-2. It is represented on general-grid subsets for various time slices in edge-plasma, plasma-profile, and wall-physics data, with one scalar value per element in the grid subset, stored as a one-dimensional array; the edge-plasma and plasma-profile arrays are indexed from 1 to N. For edge-plasma and plasma-profile data, the timebase must be a subset of the ggd_fast timebase if the ggd_fast array of structures is used.
record.documentation:
Toroidal total current density is the signed local projection of the net [current density](name:current_density) onto the toroidal direction. It combines all included contributions before or after projection onto that same direction.

The projection and aggregation are defined by:

$$
j_\phi = \hat{\phi}\cdot\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{tot}} = \sum_k \hat{\phi}\cdot\mathbf{j}_k
$$

where $j_\phi$ is the toroidal total current density, $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{tot}}$ is the total current-density vector, $\mathbf{j}_k$ is an included current-density contribution, and $k$ labels those contributions. The unit vector $\hat{\phi}$ points toward increasing toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The total is an algebraic sum, not a sum of magnitudes, and does not select a particular species, charge state, or current-generation mechanism. The quantity is local, with no restriction to a particular plasma region; it is neither a current-density magnitude nor a flux-surface average or spatially integrated current.

This quantity specializes [total current density](name:total_current_density) by fixing its common signed projection to the toroidal direction. The adjacent [radial total current density](name:radial_total_current_density) instead projects the same net charge-flux density onto the outward major-radius direction.

Sign convention: Positive when the net conventional charge transport is in the direction of increasing toroidal angle, counterclockwise when viewed from above along the negative vertical direction.
record.name: toroidal_total_current_density

record.description: Toroidal reference magnetic field is the signed toroidal component of the equilibrium magnetic field at the reference point whose major radius is the reference major radius, expressed in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
record.documentation:
Toroidal reference magnetic field is the signed toroidal component of the equilibrium magnetic field at a specified reference point in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The reference point has major radius equal to the [reference major radius](name:reference_major_radius).

The defining projection is:

$$
B_{\phi,\mathrm{ref}} = \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{eq}}(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{ref}}) \cdot \hat{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{ref}})
$$

where $B_{\phi,\mathrm{ref}}$ is the toroidal reference magnetic field, $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{eq}}$ is the equilibrium magnetic field, $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{ref}}=(R_{\mathrm{ref}},\phi_{\mathrm{ref}},Z_{\mathrm{ref}})$ is the full reference point in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $R_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the reference major radius, and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing $\phi$. For an axisymmetric equilibrium, the value is independent of $\phi_{\mathrm{ref}}$.

This quantity is the reference-location specialization of [toroidal magnetic field](name:toroidal_magnetic_field). It is distinct from [toroidal magnetic field at magnetic axis](name:toroidal_magnetic_field_at_magnetic_axis), from the magnetic-field magnitude, and from [toroidal vacuum magnetic field](name:toroidal_vacuum_magnetic_field).

Sign convention: Positive when $B_\phi$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.
record.name: toroidal_reference_magnetic_field

record.description: Total non-inductive power coupled from external neutral-beam and radio-frequency (electron-cyclotron, ion-cyclotron, and lower-hybrid) heating systems to the plasma, summed over auxiliary sources and excluding Ohmic heating. Values are represented as a one-dimensional array and expressed in W.
record.documentation:
Total external heating power is the aggregate non-inductive power coupled to the plasma by auxiliary heating systems. It includes neutral-beam injection and electron-cyclotron, ion-cyclotron, and lower-hybrid systems, while excluding power associated with Ohmic induction.

The defining aggregate relation is

$$
P_{\mathrm{ext}} = \sum_{s \in \mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{aux}}} P_s
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{ext}}$ is the total external heating power, $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{aux}}$ is the set of included auxiliary heating systems, and $P_s$ is the power coupled to the plasma by auxiliary source $s$.

The quantity applies to the whole plasma and is summed over all included auxiliary sources rather than resolved by source, species, or spatial region. It represents external power input that may contribute to both plasma heating and non-inductive current drive; it is distinct from Ohmic heating and from generator power that is not coupled to the plasma. Source-specific contributions include [total power due to electron-cyclotron heating](name:total_power_due_to_electron_cyclotron_heating), [total power due to ion-cyclotron heating](name:total_power_due_to_ion_cyclotron_heating), and power absorbed from a neutral-beam injector, whose aggregate forms contribute to the sum.
record.name: total_external_heating_power

record.description: Signed vertical position of the plasma-current centroid, obtained by weighting the toroidal current distribution by height in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, integrating over the poloidal plasma cross-section and normalizing by total plasma current at each equilibrium time slice; expressed in m.
record.documentation:
The vertical coordinate of the plasma-current center is the current-density-weighted centroid height of the plasma current distribution in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

$$
Z_{\mathrm{c}} = \frac{\int_{\mathcal{A}} Z\,j_{\phi}(R,Z)\,dA}{\int_{\mathcal{A}} j_{\phi}(R,Z)\,dA}
$$

where $Z_{\mathrm{c}}$ and $Z$ are vertical coordinates in m, $R$ is major radius in m, $j_{\phi}$ is toroidal current density in A m$^{-2}$, $dA$ is differential poloidal cross-sectional area in m$^{2}$, and $\mathcal{A}$ is the region carrying plasma current. The current-weighted center is distinct from the geometric axis; its radial counterpart is the [radial coordinate of the current center](name:radial_coordinate_of_current_center).

Sign convention: Positive when the plasma-current centroid lies in the $+Z$ direction from the coordinate origin.
record.name: vertical_coordinate_of_current_center

record.documentation:

The coordinate is defined by

$$
Z = \mathbf{x}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{z}}
$$

where $\mathbf{x}$ is the position vector of the constraint position measured from the coordinate origin, and $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$ is the upward unit vector along the symmetry axis.

This quantity applies individually at each constraint position. It is a point coordinate, not a spatial average of position or the value of the constrained physical observable.

The same vertical projection defines the [vertical coordinate of a measurement position](name:vertical_coordinate_of_measurement_position), while this quantity is specifically evaluated at the constraint position.

Sign convention: Positive when the constraint position lies above the zero-height plane along the upward unit vector $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$.

record.documentation:
Vertical coordinate of a plasma filament geometry point specifies its signed height in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. Here $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is the vertical coordinate parallel to the toroidal symmetry axis.

The coordinate is defined by:

$$
Z = \mathbf{x}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{z}}
$$

where $\mathbf{x}$ is the position vector of the specified point relative to the coordinate origin and $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$ is the unit vector along the positive symmetry-axis direction.

The specified point is the reference point for an oblique cross-section or the second endpoint of the central segment for a thick-line cross-section. record.documentation: Toroidal magnetic flux at the selected plasma boundary is the net flux of the toroidal magnetic-field component through the poloidal cross-section enclosed by the selected plasma boundary. It is the boundary value of toroidal magnetic flux used to define toroidal-flux radial labels. Here the selected boundary is the magnetic flux surface used by fixed-boundary codes, typically chosen at psi_norm = 99.x% of the separatrix, rather than necessarily the last closed magnetic flux surface. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height, the boundary toroidal flux is defined by $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor},b} = \int_{\Omega_b} \mathbf{B}\cdot\hat{\phi}\, dA_{RZ} = \int_{\Omega_b} B_\phi(R,Z)\, dA_{RZ} = \int_{\Omega_b} F(\psi(R,Z))/R\, dA_{RZ}$, where $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor},b}$ is this boundary toroidal flux, $\Omega_b$ is the selected-boundary-enclosed region in the poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field, $B_\phi$ is its toroidal component in tesla, $dA_{RZ}$ is the poloidal cross-sectional area element in square meters, $F(\psi)=R B_\phi$ is the poloidal-current function in tesla meters, and $\psi$ is the equilibrium poloidal magnetic-flux label. It also differs from [poloidal magnetic flux at the plasma boundary](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary), which is magnetic flux through a horizontal disk rather than through the boundary-enclosed poloidal cross-section. Sign convention: Positive when the net toroidal magnetic field threading the selected-plasma-boundary poloidal cross-section points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$. The quantity is evaluated at each equilibrium time slice.

record.description: Weight of an interferometer beam is the scalar factor assigned to the residual for one interferometer beam, controlling how strongly that beam's line-integrated electron-density constraint contributes to a weighted objective. It applies per beam, not to an entire interferometer system.
record.documentation:
Weight of an interferometer beam is the scalar factor assigned to the residual for one interferometer beam in a weighted objective. The residual is associated with that beam's line-integrated electron-density constraint, so the weight controls that beam's relative influence among simultaneously weighted constraints.

For a quadratic weighted objective, the contribution from one beam is represented by:

$$
\Phi_b = w_b r_b^2
$$

where $w_b$ is the weight of the interferometer beam, $r_b$ is the residual between the modeled and reference line-integrated electron density for the same beam, and $\Phi_b$ is that beam's contribution to the objective.

The scope is a single interferometer beam. No summation, averaging, or normalization over multiple beams is implied; a set of beams has separate weights and separate residual contributions. This quantity is not the line-integrated electron density, not the residual itself, not an uncertainty, and not a weight for a whole interferometer system or for other constraint types.

The [equilibrium weight of an interferometer beam](name:equilibrium_weight_of_interferometer_beam) is the equilibrium-specific specialization of this parent quantity. Changing $w_b$ changes only the relative contribution of the corresponding beam term in the objective; it does not change the definition of the beam residual.
record.name: weight_of_interferometer_beam

record.description: The signed y component of the unit vector along the major axis of an elliptic shatter cone is its projection in the right-handed Cartesian (x, y, z) frame.
record.documentation:
The signed y component of the unit vector along the major axis of an elliptic shatter cone is the projection of that major-axis direction onto the $y$ basis direction of the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ frame. The major-axis direction is the orientation of the principal semiaxis of the cone's elliptic cross-section.

The component is defined by

$$
e_{\mathrm{maj},y} = \hat{e}_{\mathrm{maj}} \cdot \hat{y}
$$

where $e_{\mathrm{maj},y}$ is the y component of the shatter-cone major-axis unit vector, $\hat{e}_{\mathrm{maj}}$ is the unit vector along the major axis of the elliptic shatter cone, and $\hat{y}$ is the y basis vector of the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ frame.

This quantity applies to the geometry of an elliptic shatter cone and to the major semiaxis orientation of its elliptic cross-section; its aggregation convention is none, because it is a single vector component rather than a sum or mean. It is distinct from the unsigned major-axis length, from the [y component of the shatter-cone direction unit vector](name:y_direction_unit_vector_of_shatter_cone), which describes the cone direction rather than the major-axis orientation, and from the [y component of the minor-axis unit vector](name:y_minor_axis_unit_vector_of_shatter_cone), which refers to the orthogonal minor semiaxis.

Together with the [x component](name:x_major_axis_unit_vector_of_shatter_cone) and [z component](name:z_major_axis_unit_vector_of_shatter_cone), this quantity forms the Cartesian representation of $\hat{e}_{\mathrm{maj}}$; the linked x and z components and $e_{\mathrm{maj},y}$ satisfy $(e_{\mathrm{maj},x})^2 + (e_{\mathrm{maj},y})^2 + (e_{\mathrm{maj},z})^2 = 1$, where $e_{\mathrm{maj},x}$ and $e_{\mathrm{maj},z}$ are the linked x and z components. The major-axis and minor-axis unit vectors jointly orient the elliptic cone and satisfy $\hat{e}_{\mathrm{maj}} \cdot \hat{e}_{\mathrm{min}} = 0$, where $\hat{e}_{\mathrm{min}}$ is the minor-axis unit vector with [x](name:x_minor_axis_unit_vector_of_shatter_cone), [y](name:y_minor_axis_unit_vector_of_shatter_cone), and [z](name:z_minor_axis_unit_vector_of_shatter_cone) components.

Sign convention: Positive when $\hat{e}_{\mathrm{maj}}$ has a component in the $+\hat{y}$ direction of the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ frame.
record.name: y_major_axis_unit_vector_of_shatter_cone

record.description: Thermodynamic temperature associated with a selected thermocouple sensor attached to a tokamak structural component.
record.documentation:
This quantity is the absolute thermodynamic temperature associated with one selected sensor member, represented by the thermal state at its thermocouple junction. It characterizes the local thermal condition of the attached structural component at the sensor location.

For a system in thermodynamic equilibrium, temperature is defined by

$$
T = \left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial S}\right)_{V,N}
$$

where $T$ is thermodynamic temperature, $U$ is internal energy, $S$ is entropy, $V$ is volume, and $N$ is the amount of material or particle number held fixed in the derivative.

The quantity applies to the selected sensor member individually and is not a sum, average, or other aggregation over the sensor set. It denotes the sensor or junction thermal state associated with a structural component, not the temperature of a flowing coolant or of an entire plant connection.

It is distinct from [coolant temperature at inlet](name:coolant_temperature_at_inlet), which describes fluid entering a cooling system. Object-specific quantities such as [temperature of a coil conductor](name:temperature_of_coil_conductor) and [temperature of a neutron detector](name:temperature_of_neutron_detector) apply the same thermodynamic concept to explicitly named hardware rather than to the generic sensor locus.
record.name: temperature_of_sensor

record.description: Normalized toroidal beta is the whole-plasma toroidal pressure beta rescaled by minor radius and signed reference toroidal field relative to plasma current.
record.documentation:
Normalized toroidal beta is the conventional current-and-geometry rescaling of the whole-plasma toroidal pressure beta. Its defining normalization is $\beta_{\mathrm{N}}=100\,\beta_{\mathrm{tor}}\,a[\mathrm{m}]\,B_0[\mathrm{T}]/I_p[\mathrm{MA}]$. Here $\beta_{\mathrm{N}}$ is normalized toroidal beta, $\beta_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the dimensionless [toroidal beta](name:toroidal_beta), $a$ is plasma minor radius, $B_0$ is the signed reference vacuum toroidal magnetic field and $I_p$ is the signed net toroidal plasma current. The bracketed units specify the numerical values used in this conventional normalization.

The underlying toroidal pressure ratio, before that rescaling, obeys $$\beta = \frac{2\mu_0 \langle p\rangle}{B^2}$$ with $\beta=\beta_{\mathrm{tor}}$, $B=B_0$, $\mu_0$ vacuum permeability and $\langle p\rangle$ the whole-plasma volume average of the pressure used to form the toroidal beta. This pressure-ratio equation defines the operand $\beta_{\mathrm{tor}}$; it is not the defining equation of $\beta_{\mathrm{N}}$.

The pressure input includes the thermal and nonthermal contributions represented by the total-pressure input. A pressure estimate obtained from equilibrium reconstruction changes that pressure input rather than the normalization. Restricting the pressure input to thermal pressure defines the separately named [normalized toroidal thermal beta](name:normalized_toroidal_thermal_beta).

The normalization requires positive minor radius and nonzero reference field and plasma current. It preserves the signed ratio $B_0/I_p$ without silently replacing either by its magnitude. For nonnegative underlying toroidal beta, the sign of the normalized value follows that ratio. The normalized quantity differs from unnormalized toroidal beta by the explicit factor of 100 and the stated size, field and current factors.
record.name: normalized_toroidal_beta

record.description: Electromotive-force contribution to the plasma loop voltage caused by changing externally generated poloidal magnetic flux, including flux linked through active coils and passive conducting structures.
record.documentation:
This quantity is the inductive electromotive-force contribution to the plasma loop voltage produced by time-varying poloidal magnetic flux generated by active coil circuits and magnetically coupled passive conducting structures. It excludes resistive voltage drops and other non-inductive contributions.

The contribution is defined by Faraday's law:

$$
V_{\mathrm{ext}}(t) = -\frac{d\Phi_{\mathrm{ext}}(t)}{dt}
$$

where $\Phi_{\mathrm{ext}}$ is the externally generated poloidal magnetic flux linked by the considered toroidal plasma circuit and $t$ is time. It contributes to the total [loop voltage at the plasma boundary](name:loop_voltage_at_plasma_boundary); currents in passive conductors are represented by the linked-flux response of structures such as those described by [current of passive structure](name:current_of_passive_structure).

Sign convention: Positive when the induced electromotive force has a positive line integral in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.
record.name: external_loop_voltage

record.description: Characteristic timescale of electric-current decrease during a disruption, defined by a specified linear-threshold or exponential decay convention.
record.documentation:
This quantity characterizes electric-current decay during a disruption. It encompasses the total plasma current and the current carried by a specified particle population, without imposing a particular current component or decay convention.

For a linear threshold convention, the extrapolated full-decay time is defined by:

$$
\tau_{\mathrm{lin}}=\frac{t(f_{\mathrm{low}})-t(f_{\mathrm{high}})}{f_{\mathrm{high}}-f_{\mathrm{low}}}
$$

where $\tau_{\mathrm{lin}}$ is the linear decay time, $f_{\mathrm{high}}$ and $f_{\mathrm{low}}$ are the upper and lower fractions of a specified reference current magnitude, and $t(f)$ is the time at which the decaying current magnitude reaches fraction $f$ of that reference.

An exponential convention instead defines an e-folding time through $I(t)=I_0\exp[-(t-t_0)/\tau_{\mathrm{exp}}]$, where $I(t)$ is the selected current magnitude at time $t$, $I_0$ is its value at reference time $t_0$, and $\tau_{\mathrm{exp}}$ is the exponential decay time. A linear threshold time is not generally equal to an exponential e-folding time.

The [plasma-current decay time](name:plasma_decay_time_due_to_disruption) uses the linear construction with upper and lower fractions of 0.8 and 0.2. The [runaway-electron current decay time](name:runaway_electron_decay_time_due_to_disruption) applies to the total toroidal runaway-electron current and permits custom linear, fixed 20–80% linear, or exponential conventions. These specializations characterize different current populations and need not have equal decay times; neither denotes a local current-density decay time or an electron-temperature decay time.
record.name: decay_time_due_to_disruption

record.description: Back-surface neutron energy flux is the local rate of neutron kinetic-energy transfer outward through an object's designated rear surface, per unit actual surface area and time. It is a scalar energy flux, not a neutron count flux, integrated power, or spatial maximum.
record.documentation:
Backa-surface neutron energy flux is the local rate at which neutron kinetic energy crosses outward through an object's designated rear surface, per unit actual surface area and time. It is a scalar measure of energy transfer, not a neutron count rate.

The local energy flux is defined by

$$
\Gamma_{n,\mathrm{back}}^{E}(\mathbf r,t) = \frac{\partial^2 E_{n,\mathrm{out}}}{\partial A\,\partial t}(\mathbf r,t)
$$

where $\Gamma_{n,\mathrm{back}}^{E}$ is the back-surface neutron energy flux, $n$ identifies the neutron contributions, $\mathbf r$ is position on the back surface, $t$ is time, $E_{n,\mathrm{out}}$ is the cumulative kinetic energy carried by neutrons crossing outward through the surface, and $A$ is actual surface area.

The quantity applies locally over the object's designated back surface and aggregates the kinetic-energy contributions of outward-crossing neutrons across their energies. It excludes neutron number flux, neutron production within a volume, energy deposited inside material, power integrated over a surface, and a spatial maximum or average over the surface.

Integrating the local flux over a portion of the back surface gives the neutron power crossing outward through that portion. The [maximum of back-surface neutron flux](name:maximum_of_back_surface_neutron_flux) is the greatest local value over the applicable back surface; that maximum is not part of this local quantity.
record.name: back_surface_neutron_energy_flux

record.description: Minimum gas flow is the smallest pressure-volume gas throughput that a gas injection valve can reliably deliver, defining the lower bound of its controllable range.
record.documentation:
Minimum gas flow is the lower reliable operating limit of the pressure-volume throughput delivered by a gas injection valve. It identifies the smallest controllable value of the aggregate gas stream throughput, rather than a molecular-species flow or particle-number rate.

The pressure-volume throughput represented by this quantity is defined as

$$
Q_g = p_g \frac{dV_g}{dt}
$$

where $Q_g$ is gas pressure-volume throughput, $p_g$ is gas pressure at the flow boundary, $V_g$ is the volume of gas crossing that boundary, and $t$ is time.

This quantity applies to the aggregate gas stream delivered through an injection system across a defined flow boundary. The stream is not restricted to a particular molecular species or charge state, and this quantity is distinct from mass flow and particle-number rate. Its defining distinction is the lower reliable operating bound, rather than an unrestricted instantaneous throughput.

The gas flow quantity defines the same pressure-volume throughput without imposing a lower-limit condition; minimum gas flow is its lower reliable operating bound. Conversely, [maximum gas flow](name:maximum_gas_flow) is the upper reliable operating bound, so the two quantities delimit the controllable range rather than represent different throughput definitions.
record.name: minimum_gas_flow

$$

record.description: Non-negative curvature radius of one arc-of-circle segment used to approximate the cross-sectional contour of a poloidal field coil. The contour lies in a poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, where R is major radius and Z is vertical height.
record.documentation:
Radius of a poloidal-field-coil arc is the non-negative circle radius of a single circular segment of the coil cross-sectional contour, taken in a poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. The conductor or winding-pack boundary is approximated by connected circular arcs, and this quantity sets the local radius of curvature of one such arc.

For a circular contour segment, the curvature radius $\rho$ (in m) is the inverse magnitude of the planar curvature $\kappa$ (in m$^{-1}$) of the boundary curve in the $(R, Z)$ cross-section:

$$
\rho = \frac{1}{|\kappa|}
$$

where a finite physical arc has $\rho > 0$, and as $\rho$ grows the segment approaches a straight line ($\kappa \to 0$). Each arc is anchored by a start point in the poloidal plane: its major-radius coordinate is given by major_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil and its vertical coordinate by [height_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:height_of_poloidal_field_coil); both together with $\rho$ are needed to locate and shape one arc, with the end of each arc coinciding with the start of the next.

The value is determined from the designed circular-arc contour, from CAD geometry, or by fitting circular arcs to surveyed boundary points. Small radii represent tightly rounded corners and compact winding-pack features, while larger radii represent gently curved coil sides; the magnitude scales with coil aperture, winding-pack dimensions, and mechanical-clearance requirements. An analogous arc-of-circle convention applies to iron core segment boundaries via radius_of_iron_core_segment.
record.name: radius_of_poloidal_field_coil

Thickness of a breeder blanket layer evaluated at the midplane is the local through-thickness of that layer along the specified thickness direction, evaluated at the midplane. The quantity applies to a single material or functional layer within the blanket, not to the total breeder blanket module build.

The layer thickness is defined by the separation of the two bounding interfaces along the thickness coordinate:

$$
d_\ell = \left|s_{\ell,\mathrm{out}} - s_{\ell,\mathrm{in}}\right|
$$

It is not the toroidal width, poloidal height, surface extent, or volume-equivalent thickness of the layer. $$
P_{i,q}^{\mathrm{co}\to\mathrm{fast}} = \left\langle \int \frac{1}{2}m_i v^2 C_{i,q}^{\mathrm{coll}}\!\left[f_{i,q}^{\mathrm{fast}},f_{\mathrm{co}}^{\mathrm{fast}}\right] \, d^3v \right\rangle_{\psi}
$$

The operator $C_{i,q}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ gives the collisional time derivative of the recipient distribution due to those donors. The brackets denote the volume-shell-weighted magnetic flux-surface average, with $\psi$ labeling the surface.

Only the
 specified recipient species and charge state are included; no recipient-species or charge-state sum is implied. Counter-passing and trapped donors are excluded. Unlike [co-passing thermal-ion charge-state collisional power density](name:co_passing_thermal_power_density_due_to_coulomb_collisions_with_ion_state), this quantity concerns fast rather than thermal recipient ions. It is an energy-exchange rate, not stored kinetic-energy density or volume-integrated power.

Summing over all ionic charge states of the same recipient species gives [co-passing fast-ion collisional power density](name:co_passing_fast_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions). Its relationship to the all-orbit parent, [fast-ion charge-state collisional power density](name:fast_ion_charge_state_power_density_due_to_collisions), is an aggregation over co-passing, counter-passing, and trapped donors with the same recipient population and transfer direction. record.documentation:
The total divertor current is the algebraic conventional current delivered by charged particles crossing the plasma-facing surfaces of the complete divertor assembly. It includes ion and electron contributions and excludes neutral-particle flux and displacement current.

$$
I_{\mathrm{div}} = \int_{S_{\mathrm{div}}} \mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{ch}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}\, dA = \int_{S_{\mathrm{div}}} \sum_s q_s\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_s \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}\, dA
$$

where $I_{\mathrm{div}}$ is the total current in A, $S_{\mathrm{div}}$ is the union of divertor target surfaces, $\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{ch}}$ is conventional charged-particle current density in A m$^{-2}$, $q_s$ is the signed charge of species $s$ in C, $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_s$ is its particle flux density in m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$, and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ points from the plasma toward the material.

This assembly-integrated quantity differs from [current at a divertor target](name:current_at_divertor_target), which applies to one target, and [current of a divertor tile](name:current_of_divertor_tile), which applies to an individual tile.

Sign convention: Positive when conventional charged-particle current flows from the plasma into the divertor material.

record.description: Minor radius of the plasma boundary is half the difference between the maximum and minimum major radii on its poloidal cross-sectional contour.
record.documentation:
Minor radius of the plasma boundary characterizes the horizontal size of its poloidal cross-section. It is a nonnegative geometric [radius](name:radius) defined by the contour's full major-radius extent.

The defining relation is

$$
R_{\mathrm{minor}} = \frac{R_{\max}-R_{\min}}{2}
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{minor}}$ is the minor radius of the plasma boundary, and $R_{\max}$ and $R_{\min}$ are the maximum and minimum [major radii](name:major_radius) on its poloidal contour. These coordinates refer to the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The extrema are taken over the entire [radial outline of the plasma boundary](name:radial_outline_of_plasma_boundary), whose total major-radius span is twice this minor radius. This is a single contour-wide size parameter, not a local major-radius coordinate, a flux-surface average, or the distance from the magnetic axis to an individual boundary point. No circular-cross-section assumption is implied.

The last closed magnetic flux surface: the outermost flux surface on which field lines close on themselves, bounding the confined plasma. Where $\psi = \psi_{\mathrm{LCFS}}$, $\psi$ is poloidal magnetic flux; $\psi_{\mathrm{LCFS}}$ is its value on the last closed flux surface.

record.documentation:

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{minor}} = \frac{R_{\max}-R_{\min}}{2L_{\mathrm{ref}}}
$$

where $R_{\max}$ and $R_{\min}$ are the maximum and minimum major-radius coordinates of the surface, each in m, and $L_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the specified positive reference length in m.

The label is a geometric normalization of the surface half-width; it is not a magnetic-flux normalization and therefore is distinct from the [normalized toroidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate). Its numerical value depends on the chosen reference length.

record.description: Radial flux-surface location of the selected plasma boundary, expressed by the normalized poloidal flux coordinate. record.documentation:
The normalized poloidal flux coordinate of the plasma boundary is the value of the [normalized poloidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate) on the closed flux surface selected as the plasma boundary. It is the linear normalized poloidal flux, labeling the boundary's radial position between the magnetic axis and the last closed flux surface.

Its value is the poloidal flux difference from the magnetic axis normalized to the axis-to-separatrix flux difference:

$$
\psi_{\mathrm{N}}^{\mathrm{boundary}} = \frac{\psi_{\mathrm{boundary}} - \psi_{\mathrm{axis}}}{\psi_{\mathrm{sep}} - \psi_{\mathrm{axis}}}
$$

where $\psi_{\mathrm{boundary}}$ is the [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) on the selected plasma-boundary surface, $\psi_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is the [poloidal magnetic flux at the magnetic axis](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis), and $\psi_{\mathrm{sep}}$ is the poloidal magnetic flux at the separatrix (last closed flux surface).

The label equals zero at the magnetic axis and equals one when the selected plasma boundary coincides with the separatrix; a value below one selects an internal closed flux surface. Its defining role is to specify, for fixed-boundary equilibrium representations, which closed flux surface is taken as the plasma boundary, commonly a surface just inside the separatrix so that the boundary remains strictly closed.

This is the linear normalized poloidal flux value itself, not its square root, and it is a flux-surface label rather than a signed poloidal-flux value or a geometric minor-radius measure. It is distinct from the toroidal-flux-based boundary label normalized toroidal flux coordinate at the plasma boundary, and it belongs to the same locus-valued family as the normalized poloidal flux coordinate at minimum safety factor and the [normalized poloidal flux coordinate of the pedestal](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_pedestal).

record.description: Outer radius of a plasma filament is the geometric radius of the outer circular boundary of the annular cross-section representing a current-carrying plasma filament. It marks the external boundary of the conducting annular region.
record.documentation:
Outer radius of a plasma filament is the geometric radius of the outer circular boundary of the annular cross-section representing a current-carrying plasma filament. It marks the external boundary of the conducting annular region; material outside this boundary is not part of that annular filament cross-section.

For the outer circular boundary in the poloidal cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the outer radius $r_\mathrm{outer}$ is the distance from the filament cross-section center $(R_c, Z_c)$ to any point $(R, Z)$ on that boundary:

$$
r_\mathrm{outer} = \sqrt{(R - R_c)^2 + (Z - Z_c)^2}
$$

where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, $Z$ is vertical height, $(R_c, Z_c)$ is the center of the annular cross-section, and $(R, Z)$ lies on the outer circular boundary.

The quantity applies only to the outer boundary of an annular plasma-filament cross-section and is a single geometric radius for that boundary, not an average over the conducting region. It is the outer member of radius of a plasma filament, paired with the [inner radius](name:inner_radius_of_plasma_filament) $r_\mathrm{inner}$; by definition $0 \le r_\mathrm{inner} \le r_\mathrm{outer}$, and the current-carrying cross-section occupies the annular region between the two radii. For the same annular geometry, the area of a plasma filament $A$ satisfies $A = \pi(r_\mathrm{outer}^2 - r_\mathrm{inner}^2)$, where $A$ is the area of the annular plasma-filament cross-section and $\pi$ is the circle constant. This quantity excludes the major radius of the filament center about the toroidal symmetry axis and rectangular cross-section dimensions such as [plasma filament width](name:plasma_filament_width) and [height of a plasma filament](name:height_of_plasma_filament).
record.name: outer_radius_of_plasma_filament

record.description: Particle energy is the energy associated with particle motion, inherited by specialized forms that are either a kinetic-energy-like coordinate of a velocity-space distribution or the kinetic energy of a particle population.
record.documentation:
Particle energy is the energy associated with the kinetic motion of particles. It is the general quantity inherited by its specialized forms, which differ in whether the energy is a coordinate attached to individual particle motion or a total carried by a particle population.

For a single particle of mass $m$ moving nonrelativistically with velocity $\mathbf{v}$, the underlying kinetic energy is:

$$
W = \frac{1}{2}m|\mathbf{v}|^2
$$

where $W$ is the particle kinetic energy, $m$ is the particle mass, and $\mathbf{v}$ is the particle velocity. Specialized forms use this energy, or an equivalent velocity-space weighting, in different roles.

The general quantity does not select a species, particle population, spatial region, velocity component, or aggregation convention. It is therefore not inherently a population-integrated total, not restricted to suprathermal particles, and not inherently a gyrokinetic coordinate. It is distinct from potential energy, thermal energy defined by a temperature, and field energy.

The specialized forms each fix part of this freedom. [Effective particle energy](name:effective_particle_energy) is a species-dependent, kinetic-energy-like coordinate that parameterizes a particle velocity-space distribution in gyrokinetic theory; it is a coordinate, not a population-integrated total. [Fast-particle energy](name:fast_particle_energy) is the total kinetic energy stored in a specified suprathermal population, integrated over the plasma volume and including motion parallel and perpendicular to the local magnetic field. The first fixes a species-dependent distribution coordinate, while the second fixes a population and a volume-integrated total.
record.name: particle_energy

record.description: Poloidal arc length of a closed magnetic-flux-surface contour in an equilibrium poloidal cross-section, measuring the perimeter of that selected surface.
record.documentation:
The poloidal length is the perimeter of the closed contour formed by one selected magnetic flux surface in a poloidal cross-section. It is a geometric property of the surface boundary, rather than its enclosed area, volume, or toroidal circumference.

The contour length is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height:

$$
L_{\mathrm{pol}} = \int_{\theta_a}^{\theta_b} \sqrt{\left(\frac{dR(\theta)}{d\theta}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{dZ(\theta)}{d\theta}\right)^2}\,d\theta
$$

Here $L_{\mathrm{pol}}$ is the poloidal length, $\theta$ is any smooth parameter along the contour, $R(\theta)$ and $Z(\theta)$ are its cylindrical coordinate functions, and $\theta_a$ and $\theta_b$ are parameter values at the same contour point after one complete circuit. The contour is taken at fixed toroidal angle $\phi$.

The quantity applies to one magnetic flux surface and includes the complete closed poloidal contour, with no averaging or summation over multiple surfaces. It excludes local arc segments and geometric quantities associated with the enclosed region. The selected surface may be labeled by the [normalized poloidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate).

Unlike [elongation of a flux surface](name:elongation_of_flux_surface), which describes a scale-independent cross-sectional shape ratio, the poloidal length retains the absolute geometric scale of the contour.

record.description: Poloidal magnetic flux is the signed magnetic flux through a horizontal disk centered on the toroidal symmetry axis, labeling magnetic surfaces in axisymmetric equilibrium.
record.documentation:
Poloidal magnetic flux is the net magnetic flux through a horizontal disk centered on the toroidal symmetry axis and bounded by the toroidal circle through the evaluation point. It specializes [magnetic flux](name:magnetic_flux) by specifying the integration surface and its orientation. In axisymmetric equilibrium, its level sets define magnetic surfaces.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle increasing counterclockwise when viewed from above, and $Z$ is vertical height. The full poloidal magnetic flux is defined by

$$
\Phi_{\mathrm{p}}(R,Z) \equiv \psi(R,Z) = 2\pi \int_0^R B_Z(R',Z)\,R'\,dR'
$$

where $\Phi_{\mathrm{p}}$, also denoted $\psi$, is the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle increasing counterclockwise when viewed from above, and $Z$ is vertical height. The full poloidal magnetic flux is defined by

$$
\Phi_{\mathrm{p}}(R,Z) \equiv \psi(R,Z) = 2\pi \int_0^R B_Z(R',Z)\,R'\,dR'
$$

where $\Phi_{\mathrm{p}}$, also denoted $\psi$, is the poloidal magnetic flux, $B_Z$ is the vertical magnetic-field component, and $R'$ is the radial integration variable. The factor $2\pi$ accounts for integration around the complete toroidal circle.

This quantity includes contributions from plasma currents and external sources, unlike [external magnetic flux](name:external_magnetic_flux), which excludes the plasma-generated contribution. It is the full flux, not flux divided by $2\pi$, a normalized coordinate, or a cross-sectional average. It differs from [toroidal magnetic flux](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux), which integrates the toroidal magnetic field through a poloidal cross-section.

The [magnetic-axis value](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis) and [plasma-boundary value](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary) are evaluations of this same function and provide the endpoint references for poloidal-flux normalization. For nested surfaces enclosing positive toroidal plasma current flowing toward increasing $\phi$, the poloidal flux decreases from the magnetic axis to the plasma boundary.

Sign convention: Positive when the magnetic field threading the horizontal disk has a net component toward increasing $Z$, along the upward surface normal.
record.name: poloidal_magnetic_flux

record.description: Poloidal beta compares volume-averaged total perpendicular plasma pressure with an effective poloidal magnetic-pressure scale set by net plasma current and plasma geometry.
record.documentation: Poloidal beta compares the volume-averaged plasma pressure with a current-based poloidal magnetic-pressure scale. Its source normalization is $\beta_p=4\int_V p\,dV/(R_0\mu_0 I_p^2)$. Here $p$ is the pressure supplied by the plasma or equilibrium representation, $V$ is the evaluation volume, $R_0$ is the reference major radius, $\mu_0$ is vacuum permeability and $I_p$ is the plasma current used by that normalization. The global value uses the plasma volume; a profile reports the source's specified evaluation volume. Writing $\langle p\rangle_V=V^{-1}\int_Vp\,dV$, the same quantity obeys the canonical beta relation $$\beta = \frac{2\mu_0 \langle p\rangle}{B^2}$$ with $\beta=\beta_p$, $\langle p\rangle=\langle p\rangle_V$ and $B=B_{p,\mathrm{ref}}$. The effective reference field satisfies $B_{p,\mathrm{ref}}^2=\frac{\mu_0^2I_p^2R_0}{2V}$. The reference field is an effective current-based scale rather than a pointwise poloidal field. The normalization requires nonzero $I_p$ and positive evaluation volume. It is neither an average of local pressure-to-field ratios nor an unnormalized pressure. Unlike [toroidal beta](name:toroidal_beta), it uses the current-based poloidal scale.

\Phi_{\mathrm{p},a} = \Phi_{\mathrm{p}}(R_a,Z_a) = 2\pi \int_0^{R_a} B_Z(R',Z_a)\,R'\,dR'
$$

where $\Phi_{\mathrm{p},a}$ is the magnetic-axis poloidal flux, $\Phi_{\mathrm{p}}$ is the equilibrium poloidal magnetic-flux function, $R_a$ and $Z_a$ are the magnetic-axis coordinates, $R'$ is the major-radius integration variable, and $B_Z$ is the vertical magnetic-field component.

record.description: Total power deposited on a divertor target by recombination processes, summing the plasma-ion and neutral-particle recombination channels at the plasma-material interface.
record.documentation:
This quantity captures the combined recombination power delivered to a single divertor target, encompassing two physically distinct contributions: energy released when plasma ions recombine at or near the target surface (the plasma channel, quantified by plasma_power_at_divertor_target_due_to_recombination) and energy deposited when neutral particles undergo recombination into lower-energy bound states at the material wall (the neutral channel, quantified by [neutral_power_at_divertor_target_due_to_recombination](name:neutral_power_at_divertor_target_due_to_recombination)).

The total recombination power at the target decomposes additively:

$$
P_{\rm rec,target} = P_{\rm rec,plasma} + P_{\rm rec,neutral}
$$

where $P_{\rm rec,plasma}$ is the ion-recombination contribution and $P_{\rm rec,neutral}$ is the neutral-particle recombination contribution, both in W.

This target-localized quantity is a spatial specialization of the volume-integrated [power_due_to_recombination](name:power_due_to_recombination), which integrates recombination power over the full plasma domain. In attached divertor operation, recombination power at the target is a minor fraction of the total heat load; in detached or high-recycling regimes, surface and volumetric recombination become significant energy sinks that reduce the conducted and convected flux reaching the target. It is inferred from edge plasma simulations or from particle flux measurements combined with surface energy-release models, and is non-negative by definition.
record.name: power_at_divertor_target_due_to_recombination

record.documentation:
This quantity is the signed major-radius offset between a measurement position mapped along its magnetic flux surface to the outboard midplane and the separatrix at that locus.

The defining relation is

$$
\Delta R_{\mathrm{sep,mid}} = R_{\mathrm{mapped}} - R_{\mathrm{sep,mid}}
$$

where $\Delta R_{\mathrm{sep,mid}}$ is the signed separation, $R_{\mathrm{mapped}}$ is the major radius of the mapped measurement position, and $R_{\mathrm{sep,mid}}$ is the major radius of the separatrix intersection at the outboard midplane. Both radii are coordinates in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is distance from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The mapping preserves the magnetic flux label of the original measurement position. The result is a difference of major radii, not the [radial coordinate assigned to a flux surface](name:radial_coordinate_of_flux_surface), an unmapped local separation, or the shortest distance normal to the separatrix. It vanishes on the separatrix and is negative on the confined-plasma side.

Sign convention: Positive when the mapped measurement position has a larger major radius than the separatrix at the outboard midplane, corresponding to the scrape-off-layer side.

Safety factor at magnetic axis

In axisymmetry, or using straight-field-line flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, the neighboring-surface [safety factor](name:safety_factor) is defined by

$$
q = \frac{1}{2\pi}\oint \frac{\mathbf{B}\cdot\nabla\phi}{\mathbf{B}\cdot\nabla\theta}\,d\theta
$$

where $q$ is the signed safety factor, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field, $\nabla$ is the spatial gradient operator, $\rho$ is a monotonic flux-surface label vanishing at the magnetic axis, $\theta$ is the poloidal angle, and $\phi$ is the toroidal angle. The integral covers one complete poloidal circuit. The toroidal angle belongs to the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height; increasing $\phi$ is counterclockwise when viewed from above.

The axis value $q_0$ is defined by the limit $q_0 = \lim_{\rho\to0}q(\rho)$, rather than by direct evaluation of the poloidal-angle integral at the axis. It is a locus-specific value, not a spatial average or a sum. It is also distinct from the [minimum safety factor](name:minimum_safety_factor), which selects the signed value where the winding magnitude is smallest and need not occur at the magnetic axis.

Sign convention: Positive when the toroidal angle advance of a magnetic field line is in the direction of increasing $\phi$ as the poloidal angle $\theta$ increases.

The closed magnetic-field line about which nested toroidal magnetic flux surfaces are arranged. Where $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{p}}(R_{\mathrm{axis}}, Z_{\mathrm{axis}}) = 0$, $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{p}}$ is poloidal magnetic field; $R_{\mathrm{axis}}, Z_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is the O-point inside the nested closed flux surfaces.
record.name: safety_factor_at_magnetic_axis

record.description: Spectral photon radiance is the directional photon arrival rate from plasma emission per projected area, viewing solid angle, and wavelength interval.
record.documentation:
Spectral photon radiance describes the absolute photon-number brightness of plasma radiation along a specified viewing direction, resolved by wavelength. Its spectral dependence is expressed per wavelength interval, not per frequency or photon-energy interval.

The defining differential relation is:

$$
dN_{\gamma} = L_{\gamma}(\lambda)\,dt\,dA_{\perp}\,d\Omega\,d\lambda
$$

where $\gamma$ is the number of photons crossing a collecting surface, $L_{\gamma}(\lambda)$ is the spectral photon radiance at wavelength $\lambda$, $t$ is time, $A_{\perp}$ is the collecting surface's projected area perpendicular to the ray direction, and $\Omega$ is the solid angle about that direction.

The quantity includes the line and continuum contributions present at the specified wavelength without selecting a particular emitting species or radiation mechanism. It is not a local volumetric photon-production rate, an electromagnetic energy radiance, or a detector count rate.

Integrating the contribution from an identified transition over its wavelength interval gives the [photon radiance at a spectral line](name:photon_radiance_at_spectral_line), rather than a wavelength-resolved radiance density. The [spectral bremsstrahlung photon radiance](name:spectral_bremsstrahlung_photon_radiance) is the contribution restricted to free-free emission.
record.name: spectral_photon_radiance

record.description: Full thickness of a rectangular plasma filament cross-section, measured along the in-plane direction normal to the filament's central segment. It is the transverse side length of the rectangle, complementing the tangential length measured along the segment.
record.documentation:
Thickness of a plasma filament is the full transverse extent of a rectangular (thick-line) filament cross-section, measured in the local plane of the element along the direction normal to the filament's central segment. The central segment lies in a poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, and the local tangential-normal basis is defined within that plane: the tangential direction follows the central segment while the normal direction is the in-plane perpendicular. It is a full side length, not a half-width.

For a rectangular filament cross-section, the cross-sectional area is the product of the two full local side lengths:

$$
A_\mathrm{fil} = L_0\, t
$$

where $A_\mathrm{fil}$ is the filament cross-sectional area in $\mathrm{m}^2$, $L_0$ is the tangential length in $\mathrm{m}$, and $t$ is the thickness in $\mathrm{m}$. When the local tangential and normal directions align with the cylindrical axes, the thickness coincides with either the width (radial $R$-direction extent) or the [height](name:height_of_plasma_filament) (vertical $Z$-direction extent) of the same rectangular cross-section.

In equilibrium filament descriptions, the thickness is set by the chosen local geometric representation of a discrete current-carrying plasma element. For a thick-line element it is specified directly as the rectangle side perpendicular to the central segment.

The value is a non-negative geometric length governed by the spatial resolution and local size of the filament representation. No universal device-independent numerical range applies; it should be interpreted relative to the associated tangential length and to neighboring filament spacing.
record.name: thickness_of_plasma_filament

record.description: Detected photoelectron rate assigned to each wavelength pixel of a spectrometer channel after electronic gain compensation and relative calibration, but before absolute radiometric calibration.
record.documentation:
This quantity is the spectrally resolved detection rate of photoelectrons produced by a spectrometer channel. It represents the channel response at an individual wavelength pixel rather than an absolutely calibrated optical emission quantity.

The rate for wavelength pixel $p$ is defined by

$$
R_p = \frac{dN_{\mathrm{pe},p}}{dt}
$$

where $R_p$ is the detected photoelectron rate for pixel $p$, $N_{\mathrm{pe},p}$ is the detected photoelectron count assigned to that pixel, and $t$ is time.

The quantity applies separately to each wavelength pixel of the spectrometer channel, with electronic gain compensation and relative channel calibration applied. It is not summed over the spectral range, and it is not an absolute radiance or photon-flux measurement.

Summing the rates over pixels that contain an absolutely calibrated optical emission quantity produces the corresponding line-integrated signal, represented by [intensity at spectral line](name:intensity_at_spectral_line). The electrical output [voltage of spectrometer channel](name:voltage_of_spectrometer_channel) is a distinct signal quantity and is not this photoelectron rate.
record.name: spectral_rate_of_spectrometer_channel

record.description: Signed azimuthal orientation angle of a poloidal magnetic-field probe’s sensitive-axis normal in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
record.documentation:
This quantity is the signed toroidal orientation of the sensitive-axis normal of a poloidal magnetic-field probe coil. It measures the normal’s departure from the poloidal plane through the orientation of its horizontal projection.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, the angle is defined by

$$
\alpha_{\mathrm{tor}} = \operatorname{atan2}(R,\phi), \qquad n_R=\mathbf{n}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{R}}, \quad n_\phi=\mathbf{n}\cdot\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}
$$

where $\alpha_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the toroidal orientation angle, $\mathbf{n}$ is the probe’s sensitive-axis unit normal, $n_R$ and $n_\phi$ are its cylindrical radial and toroidal components, and $\hat{\mathbf{R}}$ and $\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$ are the radial and toroidal unit vectors. Here $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; $\operatorname{atan2}$ returns the signed angle from the positive radial direction to the horizontal projection of $\mathbf{n}$.

The quantity applies to the geometric orientation of each poloidal magnetic-field probe coil. It is not the local plasma magnetic field, a field component, or an angle averaged over probes, turns, or field samples. The angle determines how the probe’s sensitive direction is related to the local magnetic-field vector and therefore how the measured component is projected. The corresponding toroidal orientation for a toroidal probe is defined by [toroidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe](name:toroidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe), while its independent poloidal tilt is represented by [poloidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe](name:poloidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe).

Sign convention: Positive when rotation from the positive radial direction toward the horizontal projection of the sensitive-axis normal is toward increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.
record.name: toroidal_angle_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe

record.description: Toroidal magnetic field at the magnetic axis is the signed component of the total equilibrium magnetic field in the toroidal direction, including external-coil and plasma-current contributions.
record.documentation:
Toroidal magnetic field at the magnetic axis is the signed toroidal projection of the total equilibrium [magnetic field](name:magnetic_field). It is evaluated locally at the magnetic axis.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, the defining projection is:

$$
B_{\phi,\mathrm{axis}} = \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{axis}} \cdot \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}
$$

where $B_{\phi,\mathrm{axis}}$ is the toroidal magnetic field at the magnetic axis, $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is the total equilibrium magnetic-field vector at that locus, and $\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle.

The total field includes externally applied and plasma-current-generated contributions. The corresponding projection of the [vacuum magnetic field](name:vacuum_magnetic_field) excludes plasma-current contributions and is therefore a distinct quantity. This on-axis value is neither a magnetic-field magnitude nor a flux-surface average.

Sign convention: Positive when the magnetic field at the magnetic axis projects in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, counterclockwise when viewed from above.
